r:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d
\]
及其逆可以被所选网络类在相关码集上表示，则
\[
f'(u)=r(f(u)),
\qquad
g'(z')=g(r^{-1}(z'))
\]
产生相同复合重构。没有额外约束，观测重构目标无法偏爱这样一种坐标系。
有限网络还承认更特定对称性：

隐藏单元可以被置换并在相邻权重矩阵中补偿；
符号变化可以对兼容奇或线性激活补偿；
正缩放可以跨正齐次层（如 ReLU 层）移动；
冗余或死单元可以改变参数而不改变实现映射；以及
等函数参数化可以来自多条优化路径。

对线性自编码器，即使主重构子空间唯一确定，编码器与解码器因子也不唯一 (Baldi 和 Hornik 1989年)。对非线性自编码器，等价可以超出旋转与缩放，延伸到架构支持的非线性瓶颈重参数化。
因此轴名、排序与码空间中的欧氏距离不被本征辨识。跨种子对齐可以辅助比较，但不确立唯一生物坐标。

title: 有界自编码器基线
text:
训练均值： 用训练均值重构每个观测。这是 \(d=0\) 参考。
PCA： 使用相同训练预处理与 MSE 几何的所需秩 \(d\) 解析线性重构基线。
线性自编码器： 使用相同瓶颈与可比层布局、恒等激活。在良好优化的全局解下应接近 PCA 主子空间重构，提供实现对照。
因子分析： 具有潜分布、对角特征特定残差协方差、似然与条件潜推断的静态概率潜变量比较。确定性自编码器没有这些概率量，不应继承其解读。
冻结随机编码器： 保持架构匹配随机编码器固定，只训练解码器，并跨种子重复。这检验学习编码是否优于通用非线性特征。
容量匹配替代： 比较声明宽度、参数数、优化预算与正则化，而非把每个增益归因于非线性。

只击败均值而未击败 PCA 的自编码器没有演示有用非线性重构。对 PCA 的非线性增益是所述架构与分布下留出 MSE 的证据，不是流形或机制的证据。

title: 有界自编码器基线
text:
防泄漏评估应包括：

独立划分单元： 按需要留出完整试次、轨迹、受试者、会话或条件。依赖重要时，不应把一条轨迹的相邻时间点散落到折叠中。
仅训练预处理： 在训练划分内拟合中心化、缩放、插补与特征选择。
仅验证选择： 用验证数据选择瓶颈、宽度、激活、正则化、轮次与种子，最好在探索许多候选时使用嵌套评估。
未触碰测试重构： 报告 \[
\operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{test}}
=
\frac{1}{|I_{\mathrm{test}}|}
\sum_{i\in I_{\mathrm{test}}}
\left\lVert
u_i-g_{\hat\phi}(f_{\hat\theta}(u_i))
\right\rVert_2^2,
\] 连同逐特征与原始单位残差摘要。
泛化差距： 报告训练、验证与测试损失，而不仅是所选测试得分。
种子稳定性： 报告跨预先声明随机种子的分布，并区分最佳验证选择与平均表现。
基线与对照： 比较均值、秩匹配 PCA、线性自编码器、冻结随机编码器与容量匹配变体。
码诊断： 报告活跃坐标方差、重复/死单元与对预处理的敏感性。码图是诊断性的，其本身不是证据。
分布移位： 在科学相关时执行受试者、会话、条件或采集留出检验，而不仅是分布内随机划分。
次级任务： 在嵌套训练规程内拟合下游预测器。解码表现是单独准则，不把重构表示验证为机制。

PCA 与自编码器损失必须在相同变换度量中计算。因子分析应主要用留出似然或预测分布评判；其条件均值重构可以次要报告，但它是依赖模型的，且不等价于确定性 MSE 训练。

title: 有界自编码器基线
text:
未来的非可执行玩具模型应采样标量参数 \(s\) 并通过
\[
x(s)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
s\\
s^2\\
0.3\sin(2s)
\end{pmatrix}
+
\varepsilon,
\]
在 \(\mathbb R^3\) 中生成观测，具有声明有界 \(s\) 范围与各向同性观测噪声。生成记录应保留 \(s\)，但 PCA 与自编码器在拟合期间都不得使用它。
比较均值预测器、秩一 PCA、秩一线性自编码器、带一维瓶颈的固定小非线性自编码器与冻结随机编码器对照。用验证观测选择轮次与正则化，并在独立采样的 \(s\) 值上评估留出 MSE。记录多个种子、死码频率与码随 \(s\) 的单调性，仅作为生成侧诊断。
必需阴性对照包括：独立全维高斯数据（一维弯曲解释在其中为假）；在极少数点上训练的高容量架构以暴露记忆；以及移位测试 \(s\) 范围以暴露外推失败。即使非线性自编码器比 PCA 更好地重构弯曲示例，有效结论也限于该模拟器与损失。本方法对象不创建数据、代码或结果。

title: 有界自编码器基线
text:
有界自编码器是 LDG 的规范确定性非线性重构基线。它询问有限非线性函数类是否在考虑关于几何、概率或动力学的更强主张之前改善留出重构。






警告这并不蕴含



低重构误差或吸引人的瓶颈可视化不证明流形、不确立本征维数、不识别唯一潜坐标、不发现动力学、不恢复机制，也不支持因果解读。窄码是架构选择；非线性解码器像是拟合函数；两者都不自动是系统的真实状态空间。




不保留模态特定经验主张。前馈自编码器可以重构固定轨迹摘要或窗口，但它会忽略时间先后，不确立行为状态、运动动力学或机制。



不保留模态特定经验主张。注视样本、事件摘要与对齐窗口定义不同重构问题；有序码不识别动眼坐标或因果控制变量。



不保留模态特定经验主张。通道缩放、重参考、伪迹处理、受试者划分与传感器几何将决定损失；瓶颈坐标不自动是神经源。



不保留模态特定经验主张。确定性重构基线可以检验声明传感器或单元特征的非线性压缩，但留出单元、试次、条件与会话是不同泛化问题。重构单独不确立神经流形或动力学。

title: 有界自编码器基线
text:
Bourlard 与 Kamp 分析多层感知机自联想及其与奇异值分解的联系，为瓶颈重构提供早期技术基础 (Bourlard 和 Kamp 1988年)。
Baldi 与 Hornik 刻画分层线性网络的平方误差景观，展示自联想主子空间解，同时指出编码器/解码器因子非唯一性 (Baldi 和 Hornik 1989年)。
Kramer 用带平方重构误差的前馈自联想瓶颈网络表述非线性主成分分析，并讨论架构容量与过拟合 (Kramer 1991年)。

title: 有界自编码器基线
text: Goodfellow、Bengio 与 Courville 提供经核查的欠完整与正则化自编码器、编码器/解码器记号、重构目标、容量与恒等复制失败的权威综合 (Goodfellow 等 2016年, chap. 14)。其中讨论的去噪、稀疏、收缩与变分扩展在此有界方法之外。

title: 有界自编码器基线
text:
哪个架构匹配对照最好地把非线性收益与参数数和优化效应分开？
当非线性重参数化保留重构时，应如何比较潜码稳定性？
哪个留出划分反映预期科学用途：试次、条件、受试者、会话还是采集系统？
何时即使特征缩放后 MSE 在科学上也不合适？
应如何在不断言把方法变成概率模型的情况下评估确定性重构的不确定性？
哪些阴性对照在下游解读之前揭示记忆或干扰重构？

title: 有界自编码器基线
text:
使用完整方法 schema 并定义有界确定性前馈方法。
声明编码器、瓶颈、解码器、有限架构与 MSE 经验风险。
覆盖验证、早停、正则化、初始化与种子选择。
排除变分、递归、动力学、对比、去噪与稀疏族。
陈述学习/固定量、顺序无感时间处理与欧氏重构几何。
覆盖非凸优化、记忆、过拟合、死单元、塌缩与分布移位。
陈述置换、缩放、符号与非线性重参数化歧义。
包含 PCA、线性自编码器、FA、随机特征与容量对照。
提供防泄漏留出评估与非可执行玩具契约。
显式拒绝流形、维数、唯一坐标、动力学、机制与因果过度宣称。
基础、线性理论、非线性与综述来源经核查与验证。
独立混合审查返回 PASS，无需修正轮次。
在发布站点审查后，人类所有者根据记录的审查决定授权稳定晋升。

title: Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
text:
A discrete-time linear-Gaussian state-space model (LGSSM) describes an ordered sequence of observations through an unobserved state that evolves linearly with Gaussian process noise and generates measurements linearly with Gaussian observation noise. It provides one joint probability model in which forecasting, state inference, sequence likelihood, and parameter learning can be defined without treating them as the same task (Ghahramani and Hinton 1996; Särkkä 2013).
This object specifies the finite-dimensional, time-invariant, discrete-time model with a fixed or externally supplied open-loop known input path. It does not present the Kalman filtering or fixed-interval smoothing algorithms, which are later Method units. Time-varying, switching, nonlinear, non-Gaussian, continuous-time, unknown-input, feedback-policy, and control-design variants are outside the bounded core.



For one sequence of length \(T\), let

\(x_t\in\mathbb R^p\) be the observed vector;
\(u_t\in\mathbb R^r\) be an optional known input or regressor; and
\(z_t\in\mathbb R^q\) be the latent state.

A reproducible analysis must declare:

the observational unit, sequence boundaries, sampling interval, ordering, and whether matrices are assumed common across sequences;
feature definitions, units, transformations, exclusions, and missing-data policy;
which inputs are fixed or externally supplied at fitting and prediction time, and when each value becomes available;
latent dimension \(q\) and its selection protocol;
whether parameters are fixed from external knowledge or learned from training sequences; and
the exact target: forecasting, filtering, smoothing, marginal likelihood, parameter learning, or simulation.

Sequences, subjects, sessions, or trials are not interchangeable replicates. Their dependence and parameter sharing must be stated.



The model specification is a parameter tuple
\[
\theta=(m_1,P_1,A,B,C,D,Q,R),
\]
with dimensions conforming to the state, input, and observation spaces. Conditional on \(\theta\), it defines:

the joint Gaussian law \(p_\theta(z_{1:T},x_{1:T}\mid u_{1:T})\);
predictive distributions for future states and observations;
filtering distributions conditioned only on observations available through the target time;
smoothing distributions conditioned on a complete declared observation interval;
the marginal sequence likelihood after integrating out \(z_{1:T}\); and
model-conditional latent-state summaries with uncertainty.

An implementation may additionally return fitted parameters, forecast means/covariances, filtered or smoothed state moments, innovations, and likelihood contributions. These outputs have different conditioning information and must be labeled accordingly.



The state carries the information needed for the next-step transition, while observations are noisy linear views of that state. The Markov factorization converts one high-dimensional trajectory distribution into an initial-state law, local transition laws, and local observation laws. Gaussian closure makes the relevant conditional and marginal distributions Gaussian, permitting exact finite-horizon inference when parameters are known (Särkkä 2013, chs. 4, 8).
The method’s value is not merely that its inferred mean trajectory looks smooth. It is that a declared stochastic temporal model yields testable predictive distributions and separates uncertainty introduced at the transition from uncertainty introduced at measurement.



The canonical input-driven model is
\[
z_1\sim\mathcal N(m_1,P_1),
\]
\[
z_{t+1}=Az_t+Bu_t+w_t,
\qquad
w_t\sim\mathcal N(0,Q),
\]
\[
x_t=Cz_t+Du_t+v_t,
\qquad
v_t\sim\mathcal N(0,R).
\]
The no-input core is recovered by omitting \(u_t\), \(B\), and \(D\). Unless explicitly generalized, the model assumes:

\(P_1,Q\succeq0\) and \(R\succ0\);
\(z_1\), every \(w_t\), and every \(v_s\) are mutually independent;
process and observation noises are independent across time;
\(A,B,C,D,Q,R\) are constant over the sequence;
the latent transition is first-order Markov;
observations are conditionally independent across time given the state path and inputs; and
inputs are fixed in advance or externally supplied without depending on contemporaneous or future observations, so they are valid conditioning variables rather than unexplained stochastic causes.

Gaussianity is stronger than specifying only means and covariances. Correlated process and observation noise, colored noise, heteroscedasticity, time-varying matrices, or history-dependent measurements require an explicit modified model rather than an informal reinterpretation of \(Q\) or \(R\).



For a fixed open-loop input path, the joint law factorizes as
\[
p_\theta(z_{1:T},x_{1:T}\mid u_{1:T})
=p_\theta(z_1)
\prod_{t=1}^{T-1}p_\theta(z_{t+1}\mid z_t,u_t)
\prod_{t=1}^{T}p_\theta(x_t\mid z_t,u_t),
\]
where
\[
p_\theta(z_{t+1}\mid z_t,u_t)
=\mathcal N(Az_t+Bu_t,Q),
\]
\[
p_\theta(x_t\mid z_t,u_t)
=\mathcal N(Cz_t+Du_t,R).
\]
This factorization defines several different conditional targets. The future input values appearing below must be known scenario values rather than controls that encode future observations:
\[
\text{forecasting:}\quad
p(z_{t+h},x_{t+h}\mid x_{1:t},u_{1:t+h}),
\]
\[
\text{filtering:}\quad
p(z_t\mid x_{1:t},u_{1:t}),
\]
\[
\text{smoothing:}\quad
p(z_t\mid x_{1:T},u_{1:T}),\quad T>t,
\]
or the full path posterior \(p(z_{1:T}\mid x_{1:T},u_{1:T})\). Kalman explicitly distinguishes smoothing, filtering, and prediction by whether the estimated state time is earlier than, equal to, or later than the final conditioning observation (Kalman 1960). The exact recursions are deliberately deferred to separate filtering and smoothing Method Objects.
The marginal likelihood is
\[
p_\theta(x_{1:T}\mid u_{1:T})
=\int p_\theta(z_{1:T},x_{1:T}\mid u_{1:T})\,dz_{1:T}.
\]
It can be factorized into one-step predictive densities,
\[
p_\theta(x_{1:T}\mid u_{1:T})
=\prod_{t=1}^{T}
p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{1:t-1},u_{1:t}),
\]
which separates sequence scoring from state-point estimation (Särkkä 2013, sec. 12.1).
Feedback-controlled data require a separate timing and policy model. A valid control \(u_t\) must be measurable from information available before the transition it drives and, when \(D\ne0\), before the contemporaneous observation \(x_t\); using \(x_t\) itself in \(u_t\) creates an algebraic loop. If future controls depend on future observations, conditioning on the realized \(u_{1:T}\) can leak future information. Policy-aware likelihoods and forecasts must instead state the nonanticipating policy and integrate or simulate controls not yet known.



Depending on the protocol, parameter learning may estimate some or all of \(m_1,P_1,A,B,C,D,Q,R\) and select \(q\). Given fitted parameters, state inference determines conditional distributions over latent states; it does not relearn the model parameters unless an explicitly joint or online-learning procedure is used.
Maximum-likelihood learning targets the observable sequence distribution after integrating over latent states. EM instead alternates between model-conditional expectations of latent sufficient statistics and parameter updates that increase the same marginal likelihood under exact steps (Ghahramani and Hinton 1996). The inferred state path is therefore an intermediate uncertain quantity, not observed training data.



The analyst fixes the state dimension or its selection search, sequence boundaries, time step, input definition, matrix structure and parameter sharing, Gaussian and independence assumptions, covariance constraints, initial-state treatment, missing-data mechanism, learning criterion, regularization or priors, and evaluation target.
When some matrices come from physical modeling, the fixed-versus-estimated partition must be explicit. Calling \(A\) “the dynamics” does not establish that it is a physical law if \(C\), \(Q\), \(R\), state coordinates, or inputs are learned phenomenologically.



Time is discrete and ordered. Permuting observations generally changes the likelihood. The first-order Markov assumption states that, conditional on \(z_t\) and the known input, \(z_{t+1}\) does not depend on earlier states. It does not imply that the observed sequence is first-order Markov.
Stability and stationarity are distinct. For the time-invariant no-input mean dynamics, \(\rho(A)<1\) is the usual Schur-stability condition under which deterministic perturbations decay. With zero mean, constant \(Q\), and suitable finite covariance, a stable \(A\) supports a stationary state covariance \(\Sigma\) satisfying
\[
\Sigma=A\Sigma A^\top+Q.
\]
The process is stationary only when its initialization and inputs are also compatible with the stationary law. A stable model initialized away from that law has a transient; a unit-root or unstable finite-horizon model can still define valid distributions without being stationary. Time-varying inputs can make means nonstationary even when \(A\) is stable.
Irregular sampling cannot be handled by silently treating every index gap as equal. It requires gap-dependent transitions, an underlying continuous-time model and discretization, or another explicit variant.



The latent state is represented in a finite-dimensional vector space. \(A\) is linear in the chosen state coordinates, while \(Q\) and \(R\) define coordinate-dependent Mahalanobis uncertainty. Euclidean distances between posterior state means have no invariant scientific meaning unless a metric and coordinate convention are justified.
The model does not posit a nonlinear manifold or Riemannian geometry. A low-dimensional linear latent state is a modeling choice, not proof of intrinsic dimension or a unique state space.



Likelihood-based fitting from observation sequences is unsupervised with respect to external labels. Fixed open-loop inputs condition the transition and observation laws; their presence is not automatically “supervision” in the prediction-label sense. Labels, outcomes, or interventions used to design states, constrain matrices, select hyperparameters, or score models introduce task dependence and must be declared.
An observational input correlated with unmodeled disturbances is not automatically exogenous. Including \(u_t\) does not identify the causal effect represented by \(B\) or \(D\). Feedback-dependent inputs require the policy-aware extension delimited above rather than the open-loop conditional factorization used here.



For known parameters, finite-horizon linear-Gaussian forecasting, filtering, and smoothing are exact Gaussian conditioning problems. They differ only in target and information set, but require distinct computations. Filtering uses data through the current time; fixed-interval smoothing uses future observations within the declared interval (Särkkä 2013, chs. 4, 8).

The likelihood is generally nonconvex in a free latent parameterization. Initializations, covariance constraints, regularization, stopping criteria, multiple starts, and numerical factorizations must be reported. An increasing EM objective does not prove global optimality or scientific validity.




It defines a coherent joint distribution over ordered latent and observed sequences.
Process and observation uncertainty are represented separately through \(Q\) and \(R\).
Exact Gaussian forecasts and state posteriors are available when parameters are fixed.

Wrong latent dimension or structure: omitted modes leave temporal residual structure; redundant modes create weakly identified or unused states.
Noise tradeoff: short, weakly observed sequences may not distinguish process variation from observation variation, so \(Q\), \(R\), \(C\), and the state path can compensate for one another.
Unmodeled dependence: colored, correlated, heteroscedastic, or state-dependent noise invalidates the white independent Gaussian assumptions.
Nonlinearity or regime changes: one global \(A\) and \(C\) cannot represent switching, saturation, curved observation maps, or abrupt interventions.
Instability or near-unit roots: forecasts can diverge or become highly uncertain, and parameter estimates can be sensitive in short records.
Unobservable modes: latent directions that do not affect available observations cannot be recovered from those observations.
Weak excitation: inputs or process noise may fail to explore directions needed to estimate transition effects.
Missingness or censoring: treating informative missing observations as ignorable can bias learning and state inference.
Boundary covariance estimates: nearly singular \(Q\), \(R\), or \(P_1\) can create numerical failure or degenerate likelihood behavior.
Local optimization: different initializations can converge to different representatives or local optima.
Leakage: smoothing future data into an online forecast, fitting preprocessing on test sequences, or splitting adjacent time points across train and test yields optimistic evaluation.
Mechanistic overreach: a predictive \(A\) can summarize conditional evolution without identifying a biological mechanism or causal transition law.




For any invertible \(T\in\mathbb R^{q\times q}\), define \(z'_t=Tz_t\). The transformed parameters
\[
A'=TAT^{-1},\quad B'=TB,\quad C'=CT^{-1},
\]
\[
m'_1=Tm_1,\quad P'_1=TP_1T^\top,\quad Q'=TQT^\top
\]
with unchanged \(D\) and \(R\) generate the same observation distribution. Sign changes, permutations, rotations, and state-coordinate scalings are special cases. Therefore individual latent axes and matrix entries are not identified without a coordinate convention; invariant predictions, transfer behavior under declared inputs, or similarity classes may be the defensible targets.
Similarity transformation is not always the only ambiguity. Nonminimal realizations can contain unobservable or unreachable states; unknown \(C,Q,R,P_1\), restricted input coverage, singular covariances, or finite sequence length can create stronger structural or practical nonidentifiability. A good optimizer cannot recover a unique parameter outside what the observation design identifies.
For deterministic pairs, observability of \((A,C)\) asks whether states can in principle be distinguished from an output history, while controllability of \((A,B)\) asks whether inputs can reach state directions. In stochastic estimation, excitation through \(Q\) and detectability/stabilizability conditions introduce related but distinct boundaries. These properties are not automatic consequences of writing an LGSSM, and they do not by themselves prove causal or physical meaning.




Training mean or independent Gaussian: ignores both latent structure and temporal dependence. The LGSSM should improve held-out predictive likelihood or calibrated forecasts before its temporal complexity is credited.
PCA: a deterministic, static, order-blind linear representation. It provides no process/observation noise split or temporal likelihood.
Factor Analysis: a static probabilistic low-rank observation model. With independent factors at each time and no state persistence, it tests whether the transition layer is needed. FA remains the canonical static probabilistic comparison.
Observation-space autoregression or persistence: predicts measurements directly without a separate latent observation map. It is often a stronger temporal baseline than a static method and tests whether latent states add value.
Known-parameter model: separates state-inference performance from errors introduced by parameter learning. Simulation studies should report both known-parameter and learned-parameter cases.




Evaluation must respect sequence order and the information set of the intended task:

split entire subjects, sessions, trials, or trajectories when dependence crosses adjacent time points;
fit preprocessing, dimension selection, parameters, and regularization on training sequences only;
for forecasting, report one- and multi-step predictive log likelihood, error, and interval calibration using no future observations beyond the forecast origin;
for filtering, evaluate \(p(z_t\mid x_{1:t})\) or observation predictions using only online information;
for smoothing, label the task retrospective and permit \(x_{t+1:T}\) only within that separately evaluated target;
report held-out marginal sequence likelihood and compare with static and observation-space temporal baselines;
inspect innovation means, covariance, autocorrelation, temporal residual structure, and sensitivity to state dimension and covariance constraints; and
under synthetic known truth, assess state and parameter recovery only after an allowed similarity alignment, while separately scoring invariant predictions and observable covariance.

Random point-wise train/test splits are generally invalid for sequence forecasting. Comparing a smoother with an online filter on the same target without acknowledging future information is also invalid. High likelihood or low state error under the assumed model does not establish that the latent coordinates are unique or mechanistic.
Missing observations can be handled by evaluating each observation update on the observed components—equivalently selecting the relevant rows and covariance submatrices—provided the missingness mechanism is ignorable under the declared analysis. Informative missingness, censoring, unknown inputs, or observation-time selection require their own model. These variants do not change the need to keep future information out of online evaluation.



Consider the scalar no-input model
\[
z_{t+1}=az_t+w_t,
\qquad
x_t=z_t+v_t,
\]
with \(w_t\sim\mathcal N(0,q)\) and \(v_t\sim\mathcal N(0,r)\). If \(|a|<1\) and
\[
z_1\sim\mathcal N\!\left(0,\frac{q}{1-a^2}\right),
\]
then the latent process is stationary with
\[
\operatorname{Var}(z_t)=\frac{q}{1-a^2},
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(x_t,x_{t+h})
=a^h\frac{q}{1-a^2}\quad(h>0),
\]
and \(\operatorname{Var}(x_t)=q/(1-a^2)+r\). This separates temporal persistence \(a\), process variation \(q\), and measurement variation \(r\). Setting \(a=0\) produces temporally independent latent variables; setting \(a=1\) removes the stationary covariance formula even though a finite-horizon random-walk model remains well defined.
A future non-executable toy contract would generate multiple independent sequences with known \(a,q,r\); compare the training mean, static FA, observation-space AR(1), known-parameter LGSSM, and learned-parameter LGSSM; evaluate blocked predictive likelihood, multi-step calibration, innovation autocorrelation, filtered versus smoothed information sets, and similarity-aligned state recovery. No data, code, fitted result, or benchmark is produced in this Method Object.



The discrete-time LGSSM is LDG’s canonical probabilistic temporal latent baseline. The method provides a baseline for population recordings with ordered trials or time bins. Unit scaling, condition averaging, trial dependence, input definitions, and observation distributions must be explicit. No modality-specific empirical result is retained here.

title: Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
text:
A discrete-time linear-Gaussian state-space model (LGSSM) describes an ordered sequence of observations through an unobserved state that evolves linearly with Gaussian process noise and generates measurements linearly with Gaussian observation noise. It provides one joint probability model in which forecasting, state inference, sequence likelihood, and parameter learning can be defined without treating them as the same task (Ghahramani and Hinton 1996; Särkkä 2013).
This object specifies the finite-dimensional, time-invariant, discrete-time model with a fixed or externally supplied open-loop known input path. It does not present the Kalman filtering or fixed-interval smoothing algorithms, which are later Method units. Time-varying, switching, nonlinear, non-Gaussian, continuous-time, unknown-input, feedback-policy, and control-design variants are outside the bounded core.

title: Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
text:
The state carries the information needed for the next-step transition, while observations are noisy linear views of that state. The Markov factorization converts one high-dimensional trajectory distribution into an initial-state law, local transition laws, and local observation laws. Gaussian closure makes the relevant conditional and marginal distributions Gaussian, permitting exact finite-horizon inference when parameters are known (Särkkä 2013, chs. 4, 8).
The method’s value is not merely that its inferred mean trajectory looks smooth. It is that a declared stochastic temporal model yields testable predictive distributions and separates uncertainty introduced at the transition from uncertainty introduced at measurement.

title: Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
text:
The canonical input-driven model is
\[
z_1\sim\mathcal N(m_1,P_1),
\]
\[
z_{t+1}=Az_t+Bu_t+w_t,
\qquad
w_t\sim\mathcal N(0,Q),
\]
\[
x_t=Cz_t+Du_t+v_t,
\qquad
v_t\sim\mathcal N(0,R).
\]
The no-input core is recovered by omitting \(u_t\), \(B\), and \(D\). Unless explicitly generalized, the model assumes:

\(P_1,Q\succeq0\) and \(R\succ0\);
\(z_1\), every \(w_t\), and every \(v_s\) are mutually independent;
process and observation noises are independent across time;
\(A,B,C,D,Q,R\) are constant over the sequence;
the latent transition is first-order Markov;
observations are conditionally independent across time given the state path and inputs; and
inputs are fixed in advance or externally supplied without depending on contemporaneous or future observations, so they are valid conditioning variables rather than unexplained stochastic causes.

Gaussianity is stronger than specifying only means and covariances. Correlated process and observation noise, colored noise, heteroscedasticity, time-varying matrices, or history-dependent measurements require an explicit modified model rather than an informal reinterpretation of \(Q\) or \(R\).

title: Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
text:
For a fixed open-loop input path, the joint law factorizes as
\[
p_\theta(z_{1:T},x_{1:T}\mid u_{1:T})
=p_\theta(z_1)
\prod_{t=1}^{T-1}p_\theta(z_{t+1}\mid z_t,u_t)
\prod_{t=1}^{T}p_\theta(x_t\mid z_t,u_t),
\]
where
\[
p_\theta(z_{t+1}\mid z_t,u_t)
=\mathcal N(Az_t+Bu_t,Q),
\]
\[
p_\theta(x_t\mid z_t,u_t)
=\mathcal N(Cz_t+Du_t,R).
\]
This factorization defines several different conditional targets. The future input values appearing below must be known scenario values rather than controls that encode future observations:
\[
\text{forecasting:}\quad
p(z_{t+h},x_{t+h}\mid x_{1:t},u_{1:t+h}),
\]
\[
\text{filtering:}\quad
p(z_t\mid x_{1:t},u_{1:t}),
\]
\[
\text{smoothing:}\quad
p(z_t\mid x_{1:T},u_{1:T}),\quad T>t,
\]
or the full path posterior \(p(z_{1:T}\mid x_{1:T},u_{1:T})\). Kalman explicitly distinguishes smoothing, filtering, and prediction by whether the estimated state time is earlier than, equal to, or later than the final conditioning observation (Kalman 1960). The exact recursions are deliberately deferred to separate filtering and smoothing Method Objects.
The marginal likelihood is
\[
p_\theta(x_{1:T}\mid u_{1:T})
=\int p_\theta(z_{1:T},x_{1:T}\mid u_{1:T})\,dz_{1:T}.
\]
It can be factorized into one-step predictive densities,
\[
p_\theta(x_{1:T}\mid u_{1:T})
=\prod_{t=1}^{T}
p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{1:t-1},u_{1:t}),
\]
which separates sequence scoring from state-point estimation (Särkkä 2013, sec. 12.1).
Feedback-controlled data require a separate timing and policy model. A valid control \(u_t\) must be measurable from information available before the transition it drives and, when \(D\ne0\), before the contemporaneous observation \(x_t\); using \(x_t\) itself in \(u_t\) creates an algebraic loop. If future controls depend on future observations, conditioning on the realized \(u_{1:T}\) can leak future information. Policy-aware likelihoods and forecasts must instead state the nonanticipating policy and integrate or simulate controls not yet known.

title: Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
text:
Depending on the protocol, parameter learning may estimate some or all of \(m_1,P_1,A,B,C,D,Q,R\) and select \(q\). Given fitted parameters, state inference determines conditional distributions over latent states; it does not relearn the model parameters unless an explicitly joint or online-learning procedure is used.
Maximum-likelihood learning targets the observable sequence distribution after integrating over latent states. EM instead alternates between model-conditional expectations of latent sufficient statistics and parameter updates that increase the same marginal likelihood under exact steps (Ghahramani and Hinton 1996). The inferred state path is therefore an intermediate uncertain quantity, not observed training data.

title: Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
text:
The analyst fixes the state dimension or its selection search, sequence boundaries, time step, input definition, matrix structure and parameter sharing, Gaussian and independence assumptions, covariance constraints, initial-state treatment, missing-data mechanism, learning criterion, regularization or priors, and evaluation target.
When some matrices come from physical modeling, the fixed-versus-estimated partition must be explicit. Calling \(A\) “the dynamics” does not establish that it is a physical law if \(C\), \(Q\), \(R\), state coordinates, or inputs are learned phenomenologically.

title: Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
text:
Time is discrete and ordered. Permuting observations generally changes the likelihood. The first-order Markov assumption states that, conditional on \(z_t\) and the known input, \(z_{t+1}\) does not depend on earlier states. It does not imply that the observed sequence is first-order Markov.
Stability and stationarity are distinct. For the time-invariant no-input mean dynamics, \(\rho(A)<1\) is the usual Schur-stability condition under which deterministic perturbations decay. With zero mean, constant \(Q\), and suitable finite covariance, a stable \(A\) supports a stationary state covariance \(\Sigma\) satisfying
\[
\Sigma=A\Sigma A^\top+Q.
\]
The process is stationary only when its initialization and inputs are also compatible with the stationary law. A stable model initialized away from that law has a transient; a unit-root or unstable finite-horizon model can still define valid distributions without being stationary. Time-varying inputs can make means nonstationary even when \(A\) is stable.
Irregular sampling cannot be handled by silently treating every index gap as equal. It requires gap-dependent transitions, an underlying continuous-time model and discretization, or another explicit variant.

title: Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
text:
The latent state is represented in a finite-dimensional vector space. \(A\) is linear in the chosen state coordinates, while \(Q\) and \(R\) define coordinate-dependent Mahalanobis uncertainty. Euclidean distances between posterior state means have no invariant scientific meaning unless a metric and coordinate convention are justified.
The model does not posit a nonlinear manifold or Riemannian geometry. A low-dimensional linear latent state is a modeling choice, not proof of intrinsic dimension or a unique state space.

title: Discrete-Time Linear-Gaussian State-Space Model
text:
Likelihood-based fitting from observation sequences is unsupervised with respect to external labels. Fixed open-loop inputs condition the transition and observation laws; their presence is not automatically “supervision” in the prediction-label sense. Labels, outcomes, or interventions used to design states, constrain matrices, select hyperparameters, or score models introduce task dependence and must be declared.
An observational input correlated with unmodeled disturbances is not automatically exogenous. Including \(u_t\) does not identify the causal effect represented by \(B\) or \(D\). Feedback-dependent inputs require the policy-aware extension delimited above rather than the open-loop conditional factorization used here.

title: Kalman Filtering
text:
Kalman filtering sequentially computes the current latent-state distribution in a declared linear-Gaussian state-space model (LGSSM), using only observations available through the current time. Its target at time \(t\) is
\[
p(z_t\mid x_{1:t},u_{1:t}),
\]
not a retrospective distribution that uses \(x_{t+1:T}\). The recursion alternates between a prediction based on the previous filtering distribution and the transition model, and an update based on the current observation (Kalman 1960; Särkkä 2013, ch. 4).
This object treats the model matrices and covariance parameters as fixed and known during filtering. Specifying or learning an LGSSM, filtering its state, forecasting future observations, and smoothing past states are distinct tasks. Fixed-interval Kalman smoothing is deferred to P2-U10.



Use the time-invariant, input-driven LGSSM defined in the prerequisite Method:
\[
z_1\sim\mathcal N(m_1,P_1),
\]
\[
z_{t+1}=Az_t+Bu_t+w_t,
\qquad
w_t\sim\mathcal N(0,Q),
\]
\[
x_t=Cz_t+Du_t+v_t,
\qquad
v_t\sim\mathcal N(0,R).
\]
Here \(z_t\in\mathbb R^q\), \(x_t\in\mathbb R^p\), and the optional known input is \(u_t\in\mathbb R^r\). The canonical assumptions are \(P_1,Q\succeq0\), \(R\succ0\), mutual independence of the initial state and all process and observation noises, temporal independence of the noises, and a fixed or externally supplied open-loop input path.
A reproducible filtering problem must declare:

the fixed parameter tuple \((m_1,P_1,A,B,C,D,Q,R)\) and its provenance;
state, observation, and input units and coordinate conventions;
sequence boundaries, sampling interval, and treatment of resets between sequences;
exactly when each input becomes available;
initialization at the first observation;
which observation components are available at each time and why;
numerical linear-algebra method, precision, and covariance representation; and
whether the goal is current-state inference, one-step predictive scoring, online monitoring, or an input to a separate learning procedure.

For the transition from \(t\) to \(t+1\), \(u_t\) must be known before that transition is evaluated. If \(D\ne0\), the direct-feedthrough input \(u_t\) used in the measurement mean must be available before \(x_t\) is assimilated. A control constructed from \(x_t\) itself creates a contemporaneous algebraic loop unless a separate within-step timing model is supplied. Future inputs that depend on future observations are not known conditioning variables.



At each time \(t\), the filter returns or defines:

the predicted state distribution \[
p(z_t\mid x_{1:t-1},u_{1:t})
=\mathcal N(m_{t\mid t-1},P_{t\mid t-1});
\]
the one-step predictive observation distribution \[
p(x_t\mid x_{1:t-1},u_{1:t})
=\mathcal N(\widehat x_{t\mid t-1},S_t);
\]
the innovation \(\nu_t=x_t-\widehat x_{t\mid t-1}\) and innovation covariance \(S_t\); and
the filtering distribution \[
p(z_t\mid x_{1:t},u_{1:t})
=\mathcal N(m_{t\mid t},P_{t\mid t}).
\]

The filtering mean is a model-conditional posterior mean, not an observed state. Its covariance describes uncertainty under the fixed model and conditioning information; it does not include uncertainty about learned parameters unless that uncertainty is modeled separately.



The previous filtering distribution summarizes the information in past observations needed for the next recursive step. Linear propagation plus Gaussian process noise preserves Gaussianity. The current linear-Gaussian measurement then yields a Gaussian conditional distribution. Consequently, means and covariances are sufficient for exact finite-dimensional filtering under the declared model (Särkkä 2013, secs. 4.2–4.3).
The innovation is the part of the current observation not predicted from prior observations and known inputs. Its covariance combines predicted state uncertainty projected into observation coordinates with observation noise. The Kalman gain maps this observation-space discrepancy into a state-space correction.



The recursion inherits every assumption of the LGSSM. In particular:

state evolution and observation are linear in the chosen coordinates;
the prior and noises are Gaussian;
process and observation noises are white, mutually independent, and independent of the initial state;
the Markov state and conditional-observation structure is correctly specified;
matrices and covariance parameters used by the filter are fixed during the recursion;
the input path is nonanticipating under the declared within-step timing; and
any missing-observation pattern is treated as observed/fixed and non-informative unless a missingness model is added.

Under these conditions and exact arithmetic, the recursion gives the exact Gaussian filtering distributions. Kalman’s original state-space treatment derives optimal linear estimates through orthogonal projection and explicitly distinguishes filtering, prediction, and smoothing by the estimated time relative to the latest conditioning observation (Kalman 1960). This object uses the narrower Bayesian linear-Gaussian interpretation: exactness is conditional on the stated probability model, not evidence that the model generated the scientific system.



Write \(\mathcal I_t=\sigma(x_{1:t},u_{1:t})\) for the information available after assimilating \(x_t\). Define
\[
m_{t\mid s}=\mathbb E[z_t\mid\mathcal I_s],
\qquad
P_{t\mid s}=\operatorname{Cov}(z_t\mid\mathcal I_s).
\]
No quantity below conditions on \(x_{t+1}\) or any later observation.


Before the first observation,
\[
m_{1\mid0}=m_1,
\qquad
P_{1\mid0}=P_1.
\]
This prior is part of the model. An informative external initialization must be justified independently. Replacing an unknown initial distribution by an arbitrarily huge covariance is not automatically an exact diffuse initialization and can be numerically harmful; exact diffuse variants are outside this bounded Method.



For \(t\ge2\), after filtering time \(t-1\),
\[
m_{t\mid t-1}=A m_{t-1\mid t-1}+B u_{t-1},
\]
\[
P_{t\mid t-1}=A P_{t-1\mid t-1}A^\top+Q.
\]
Thus
\[
p(z_t\mid x_{1:t-1},u_{1:t})
=\mathcal N(m_{t\mid t-1},P_{t\mid t-1}).
\]
The transition input is \(u_{t-1}\) because it drives \(z_{t-1}\mapsto z_t\). The conditioning notation includes \(u_t\) because the contemporaneous observation mean may use \(D u_t\); \(u_t\) does not retroactively drive the preceding transition.



The predicted observation mean, innovation, and innovation covariance are
\[
\widehat x_{t\mid t-1}=C m_{t\mid t-1}+D u_t,
\]
\[
\nu_t=x_t-\widehat x_{t\mid t-1},
\]
\[
S_t=C P_{t\mid t-1}C^\top+R.
\]
The predictive observation law is
\[
p(x_t\mid x_{1:t-1},u_{1:t})
=\mathcal N(\widehat x_{t\mid t-1},S_t).
\]
The Kalman gain is
\[
K_t=P_{t\mid t-1}C^\top S_t^{-1},
\]
and the filtering moments are
\[
m_{t\mid t}=m_{t\mid t-1}+K_t\nu_t,
\]
\[
P_{t\mid t}=P_{t\mid t-1}-K_tS_tK_t^\top.
\]
These are the closed-form Gaussian conditioning equations (Särkkä 2013, theorem 4.2). Implementations should solve linear systems involving \(S_t\) rather than explicitly forming \(S_t^{-1}\).



In exact arithmetic, the previous covariance update is equivalent to
\[
P_{t\mid t}=(I-K_tC)P_{t\mid t-1}.
\]
The short form can lose symmetry or positive-semidefinite structure through floating-point cancellation. The Joseph form
\[
P_{t\mid t}
=(I-K_tC)P_{t\mid t-1}(I-K_tC)^\top
+K_t R K_t^\top
\]
is algebraically equivalent when \(K_t\) is the Kalman gain and expresses the covariance as a sum of positive-semidefinite terms. Asada’s inspected implementation notes specifically use this form to reduce asymmetric covariance caused by round-off and discuss factorized covariance representations as a further safeguard (Asada 2006, sec. 4.10).
The Joseph form is not a universal numerical cure. Stable implementations should also use symmetric factorizations and solves, monitor symmetry and definiteness, and avoid explicit matrix inverses. Square-root or factorized filters propagate covariance factors and can be preferable for severe scaling or conditioning problems; they are computational realizations of the same declared filtering target, not different scientific models (Särkkä 2013, sec. 4.3; Asada 2006, sec. 4.10). Detailed square-root algorithms are outside scope.



Let \(M_t\) be a row-selection matrix that retains only the components observed at time \(t\). Define
\[
x_t^{(o)}=M_t x_t,
\quad
C_t=M_tC,
\quad
D_t=M_tD,
\quad
R_t=M_tRM_t^\top.
\]
Apply the ordinary update using \(x_t^{(o)},C_t,D_t,R_t\). This preserves correlations among the retained measurement errors. If no component is observed, skip the measurement update:
\[
m_{t\mid t}=m_{t\mid t-1},
\qquad
P_{t\mid t}=P_{t\mid t-1}.
\]
This row-selection rule is exact only when the missingness indicator contributes no additional information about \(z_t\) beyond the modeled observations and covariates. Informative dropout, threshold censoring, saturation, or state-dependent sensor failure requires an explicit observation/missingness model.



Under the canonical assumptions \(P_{t\mid t-1}\succeq0\) and \(R\succ0\), the innovation covariance \(S_t\) is positive definite. After row selection, \(R_t\succ0\) for a nonempty set of distinct retained coordinates, so a Cholesky-based solve is available in exact arithmetic.
A singular \(S_t\) indicates that the implementation has left this regular model class—for example, by using zero-noise exact constraints, duplicated deterministic measurement rows, or a semidefinite \(R\). The ordinary density and inverse formula then do not apply unchanged. Redundant rows may be removed, or a separately justified degenerate-Gaussian/constraint formulation may use support-aware generalized inverses. Adding arbitrary diagonal “jitter” changes the observation model and must not be presented as a neutral mathematical fix.
If \(S_t\) is theoretically positive definite but ill-conditioned, rescale variables, use Cholesky or another rank-revealing factorization, avoid explicit inversion, and inspect the model for nearly redundant sensors or extreme covariance scales. A failed factorization is a diagnostic, not permission to silently discard uncertainty.



For a complete \(p\)-dimensional observation and nonsingular \(S_t\), the innovation gives the one-step log predictive density
\[
\ell_t
=-\frac12\left[
p\log(2\pi)+\log|S_t|+\nu_t^\top S_t^{-1}\nu_t
\right].
\]
With partial observation, replace \(p,\nu_t,S_t\) by the retained dimension and selected quantities. Summing \(\ell_t\) gives the fixed-parameter marginal sequence log likelihood. Using this likelihood inside parameter estimation does not turn the filtering recursion itself into a parameter-learning algorithm.




With parameters fixed, the filter learns no model parameter. It computes successive conditional distributions over \(z_t\) and one-step predictive distributions over \(x_t\) from incoming observations.
The model parameters may have been set from physics, estimated on separate training sequences, or updated by a distinct algorithm. EM and likelihood optimization can call a filter internally, but the outer parameter-learning criterion and updates remain separate. Treating the filtered means as error-free observations for an unqualified second-stage fit discards posterior uncertainty and can create circular conclusions.



The analyst fixes the LGSSM structure, state dimension, parameter tuple, coordinate systems, sequence/reset policy, input timing, missingness assumptions, initialization, numerical precision, covariance representation, and any diagnostic thresholds. If parameters are estimated, the training split, estimator, constraints, and model-selection rule are fixed outside the filtering operation.
The filter does not choose \(Q\) and \(R\) by deciding how much to trust dynamics versus measurements. Those covariances are model parameters whose values require external specification or a declared estimation procedure.



Filtering is causal with respect to the declared information order: \(m_{t\mid t}\) and \(P_{t\mid t}\) depend on \(x_{1:t}\) but not \(x_{t+1:T}\). Late-arriving or revised observations require a separately declared replay, out-of-sequence update, or smoothing procedure.
The algorithm assumes the discrete sampling and sequence boundaries of the LGSSM. Unequal time gaps require gap-specific transitions and process covariances; incrementing the index as if every gap were equal changes the temporal model. Filtering does not by itself make the inferred mean trajectory dynamical evidence: its temporal structure is inherited from \(A,Q\), the initialization, and the observations.



The state occupies a finite-dimensional vector space. Prediction and update use affine maps and covariance ellipsoids in declared coordinates. \(P_{t\mid s}\) and \(S_t\) define coordinate-dependent Mahalanobis geometries for uncertainty and innovations.
Under an invertible state-coordinate change \(z'_t=Tz_t\), the moments and model matrices must transform consistently, including
\[
m'_{t\mid s}=Tm_{t\mid s},
\qquad
P'_{t\mid s}=TP_{t\mid s}T^\top,
\qquad
C'=CT^{-1}.
\]
The observable predictive law can remain unchanged while latent axes and gain entries change. Euclidean distance between filtering means, visual smoothness, or covariance ellipsoids do not establish a manifold, Riemannian geometry, intrinsic dimension, or privileged biological coordinates.



No external outcome label is required. The current measurement is evidence in a probabilistic observation model, not a supervised target in the ordinary prediction-label sense. Known inputs condition the model; they do not become labels merely by being supplied.
External labels or outcomes used to choose state dimension, matrices, covariance parameters, preprocessing, or diagnostic thresholds introduce task dependence. Such selection must occur within training/validation boundaries and be reported separately from online filtering.



For fixed parameters, filtering is recursive Gaussian inference rather than nonconvex optimization. Each step uses matrix multiplication, addition, and a solve in the innovation covariance. Computational cost and conditioning depend on state and observed dimensions and on the selected factorization.
There is no guarantee that an arbitrary software implementation reproduces the mathematical recursion. Tests should compare covariance forms, preserve symmetry, check positive-semidefinite tolerances, and verify small problems against direct joint-Gaussian conditioning. Computing a finite output without an exception is not evidence of numerical correctness.




Exact finite-horizon filtering moments under the fixed linear-Gaussian model.
Sequential processing with a fixed-size state summary rather than repeated conditioning on the entire history.
Explicit propagation of process and observation uncertainty.
One-step predictive densities and innovations suitable for scoring and diagnostics.
Natural handling of irregularly absent measurement components through declared row selection.
A transparent baseline for later smoothing and for approximate nonlinear or non-Gaussian filters.





Model misspecification: nonlinear transitions, non-Gaussian tails, colored noise, correlated process/observation noise, time-varying parameters, or omitted inputs make the declared recursion model-mismatched.
Wrong \(Q/R\) balance: underestimated process noise can make the filter overconfident in propagation; underestimated observation noise can make it chase measurements.
Bad initialization: a poorly chosen mean or covariance can dominate short sequences or interact with weak observability.
Unobservable or weakly observed directions: uncertainty can remain large or become practically ill-conditioned even when some observed coordinates fit well.
Anticipating inputs: controls or regressors containing contemporaneous/future observation information leak evidence into prediction.
Sequence leakage: carrying a posterior across independent subjects, sessions, or trials invents a transition unless continuity is part of the model.
Missingness misspecification: skipping state-dependent dropout as though it were uninformative can bias inference.
Numerical loss of symmetry or definiteness: subtraction updates, explicit inverses, poor scaling, and round-off can corrupt covariances (Asada 2006, sec. 4.10).
Singular innovation covariance: deterministic or redundant measurements can invalidate the ordinary inverse-density update.
Outliers: a Gaussian likelihood can give atypical observations excessive influence; ad hoc clipping changes the method.
Parameter plug-in certainty: conditioning on estimated parameters as though known understates total uncertainty.
Interpretive overreach: a smooth or predictive filtered path can be mistaken for a validated mechanism or unique latent trajectory.




Filtering does not repair non-identifiability of the LGSSM. If two parameter/state-coordinate specifications induce the same observable law, their filtering distributions transform within the corresponding equivalence while the observed predictive distribution can agree. Similarity transformations can change latent axes, transition entries, observation loadings, gains, and posterior means without selecting a unique scientific coordinate frame.
Observability and identifiability are related but distinct. Weak observation of a state direction can make its current conditional uncertainty large under one fixed model. Structural identifiability asks whether different model specifications induce the same observable distribution. Neither property follows from a small filtering covariance computed under assumed parameters.




Open-loop prediction: propagate \(m\) and \(P\) without measurement updates. Filtering should improve declared current-state or one-step predictive criteria when measurements contain model-consistent information.
Measurement-only estimate: where a state component is directly observed, use the current measurement or a calibrated static linear transform. This tests whether temporal propagation contributes beyond sensor smoothing.
Persistence / last observation: carry forward the most recent usable observation or state proxy. This is a minimal sequential baseline.
Static Factor Analysis: infer a latent factor independently at each time under a static observation model. It separates the contribution of the temporal transition from a probabilistic observation layer.
Direct batch Gaussian conditioning: for a short sequence, condition the full joint Gaussian distribution at once. Its current-time marginal should match the recursive filter and is an implementation oracle, not a cheaper deployment baseline.

A fixed-gain or steady-state filter is not automatically a simpler version of the finite-horizon filter: it requires conditions under which covariance/gain convergence and the chosen initialization are appropriate.



Evaluation must match the intended use and separate model fit from implementation correctness:

One-step predictive log likelihood: evaluate held-out sequences through innovation densities, with parameters and preprocessing fit only on training data.
Innovation calibration: inspect mean, variance, cross-correlation, and temporal autocorrelation of standardized innovations. Apparent whiteness is a model check, not proof of correct latent states.
State error when truth exists: in simulation or a genuinely observed-state benchmark, report time-resolved RMSE or Mahalanobis error and interval coverage. A proxy state must be labeled as a proxy.
Uncertainty calibration: under repeated data from a known simulator, compare nominal posterior coverage with empirical coverage. Plug-in parameter uncertainty must be distinguished.
Baselines: compare open-loop prediction, measurement-only, persistence, and static FA under identical splits and available information.
Missingness stress tests: evaluate declared missing-channel patterns and distinguish random masking from state-dependent dropout.
Numerical checks: compare recursive output with batch conditioning on small problems; monitor covariance symmetry, factorization failures, and sensitivity to scaling and precision.
Distribution shift: separate held-out time within a sequence from held-out trials, subjects, sessions, conditions, or acquisition systems.

Do not select parameters on the test sequences and then report the same innovations as out-of-sample evidence. Lower state RMSE or predictive loss under one simulator supports that declared criterion; it does not validate a biological mechanism.



Consider the scalar random-walk model
\[
z_1\sim\mathcal N(m_1,p_1),
\qquad
z_{t+1}=z_t+w_t,
\quad w_t\sim\mathcal N(0,q),
\]
\[
x_t=z_t+v_t,
\quad v_t\sim\mathcal N(0,r),
\]
with \(q\ge0\) and \(r>0\). At the first observation,
\[
s_1=p_1+r,
\qquad
k_1=\frac{p_1}{p_1+r},
\]
\[
m_{1\mid1}=m_1+k_1(x_1-m_1),
\qquad
p_{1\mid1}=\frac{p_1r}{p_1+r}.
\]
The next prediction is
\[
m_{2\mid1}=m_{1\mid1},
\qquad
p_{2\mid1}=p_{1\mid1}+q.
\]
This example makes the uncertainty tradeoff explicit: \(r\to\infty\) makes the update approach the prediction, whereas \(r\to0\) makes a nondegenerate direct measurement dominate. These limits describe the model, not how \(q\) or \(r\) should be chosen from data.
A future non-executable toy contract should generate independent scalar sequences with retained latent truth, compare Kalman filtering with open-loop, measurement-only, persistence, static FA where meaningful, and direct batch conditioning, and score held-out predictive density, state RMSE, and interval coverage. Required stress cases are every-third-step missing observations, misspecified \(q/r\), a wrong initial prior, an outlier, and nearly duplicate measurement rows with very different scaling. The exercise should compare the short and Joseph covariance forms against a factorized implementation in finite precision, but no code, data, figures, or result claims are created here.



Kalman filtering is LDG’s canonical online latent-state inference baseline for a discrete-time LGSSM. It operationalizes the distinction between a model, a current filtering distribution, a future prediction, and a later full-interval smoothing distribution.






WarningWhat this does NOT imply



Exact Kalman filtering under a declared LGSSM does not show that the model is correct, that the filtered mean is the true state, that latent coordinates are identifiable, that dynamics are mechanistic, or that future observations were legitimately available. Smoothness, low posterior variance, innovation fit, or predictive success alone do not establish a manifold, intrinsic dimension, causal structure, or biological mechanism.




No modality-specific empirical claim is retained. Filtering could be applied to a declared movement-state model, but inferred position, velocity, intention, and control variables require different observation and transition assumptions.



No modality-specific empirical claim is retained. Missing samples, blinks, saturation, event segmentation, and irregular timing can violate simple row-selection and equal-step assumptions.



No modality-specific empirical claim is retained. Sensor mixing, rereferencing, artifacts, spatial correlation, and nonstationarity must be represented or treated as model mismatch; a filtered latent coordinate is not automatically a neural source.



No modality-specific empirical claim is retained. Trial boundaries, unit/channel missingness, observation-noise correlations, parameter sharing, and input timing determine the filtering problem. A smooth posterior mean does not establish neural population dynamics or mechanism.





Kalman introduces the state-transition approach to linear filtering and prediction, defines filtering relative to observations through the current time, derives recursive state estimation and error-covariance equations, and treats model construction as a separate problem (Kalman 1960).





Särkkä gives the inspected Bayesian prediction/update derivation, Gaussian filtering distributions, innovation covariance, Kalman gain, covariance recursion, and the boundary between filtering and later smoothing (Särkkä 2013, ch. 4).
Asada’s inspected graduate implementation notes document round-off-driven covariance asymmetry, the Joseph stabilized covariance form, and factorized covariance representations as numerical safeguards (Asada 2006, sec. 4.10).





How should uncertainty from parameter estimation be propagated into online state uncertainty without changing the bounded fixed-parameter target?
Which innovation diagnostics are most informative under dependent missingness or deliberate experimental inputs?
When should a factorized or square-root implementation be mandatory rather than optional?
How should filters be compared when state coordinates differ by observationally equivalent transformations?
Which sequence split best tests the intended use: future time, new trials, new sessions, new subjects, or new acquisition systems?
When do robust or constrained filters solve a scientifically different problem rather than merely a numerical one?





Uses the complete Method schema and the existing discrete-time LGSSM notation.
Distinguishes prior, prediction, innovation, update, and filtering distributions.
Conditions only on observations available through the current time.
States Kalman gain, innovation covariance, likelihood contribution, and Joseph covariance update.
Declares initialization, input timing, partial-observation row selection, and missingness limits.
Covers singular and ill-conditioned innovation covariance and factorized numerical boundaries.
Separates fixed-parameter filtering from model specification, learning, forecasting, and smoothing.
States learned/fixed quantities, temporal order, geometry, supervision, and inherited identifiability.
Includes failure modes, baselines, evaluation criteria, and a non-executable analytic toy contract.
Retains no modality-specific empirical claim.
Foundational, authoritative Bayesian, and numerical-stability sources were inspected and verified.
Independent mixed review returned PASS with no correction round required.
