title: Topology
text:
A topology specifies which subsets of a set are open, thereby defining neighborhoods, continuity, convergence, and connectedness without first assigning numerical distances.



Topology describes qualitative structure preserved under continuous deformation. It is weaker than metric or Riemannian geometry: spaces can share a topology while having different distances, angles, and curvature.



Topology records which points can be approached continuously and which regions are connected. It does not say how far apart points are.



A topology \(\mathcal T\) on a set \(X\) is a family of subsets such that:

\(\varnothing,X\in\mathcal T\);
arbitrary unions of members of \(\mathcal T\) belong to \(\mathcal T\);
finite intersections of members of \(\mathcal T\) belong to \(\mathcal T\).

The pair \((X,\mathcal T)\) is a topological space. A map is continuous when preimages of open sets are open. Sutherland gives these definitions and distinguishes topology induced by a metric (Sutherland 2024).




\(X\): underlying set.
\(\mathcal T\): topology.
\(U\in\mathcal T\): open set.
\(f:X\to Y\): continuous map when open-set preimages are open.




State Space supplies the set of states to which neighborhood structure may be added.










Concept
Distinction




Metric
Assigns numerical distances and induces a topology; different metrics can induce the same topology.


Geometry
Adds quantitative length, angle, or curvature beyond topology.


Manifold
A topological space with local Euclidean structure; a smooth manifold adds compatible smooth charts.


Graph connectivity
A discrete combinatorial relation, not automatically the topology of an underlying state space.






A topology does not imply a metric, smoothness, manifold structure, a unique embedding, low dimension, curvature, or dynamical law.



The usual open intervals generate the standard topology on \(\mathbb R\). The discrete topology instead declares every subset open. The same underlying set can therefore support different topologies.



Claims about loops, connected components, or holes in latent data are topological claims. They require sampling and noise analysis and are not established by one visualization or clustering result.



Topology supplies the precise layer beneath manifolds, circles, and tori while keeping topology distinct from metric geometry.




Which topological features are stable across scales and noise?
How should sampling uncertainty affect claims about connectedness or holes?
Which null models are appropriate for topological summaries?





Sutherland provides the inspected definitions of topology, continuity, neighborhoods, and metric-induced topology (Sutherland 2024).





States the topology axioms.
Separates topology, metric, geometry, and manifold structure.
States empirical non-implications.

title: State
text:
The state of a specified system at time \(t\) is the current information its chosen description carries forward to determine or predict later evolution.



State is the point at which a description of a changing system separates relevant past from future evolution. Effects of the past that still matter must be carried in the current state; details of the past that no longer matter need not be retained separately. This makes the term stronger than “what was measured now” and more specific than “a set of variables.”
A clear state definition also assigns different roles to quantities in a model. Some quantities change as part of the system, some are measured from it, some are fixed features of the model, and some influence it from outside the chosen boundary. Confusing these roles makes later claims about dynamics difficult to interpret.



Imagine pausing a system at time \(t\). A state description is adequate if it contains the information that must be carried forward to continue the description from that time, without consulting the earlier history again. Åström and Murray express this by describing state variables as variables that summarize the past for predicting the future; they also emphasize that choosing how accurately to represent the relevant information is a modeling decision (Åström and Murray 2021, sec. 3.2).
Three qualifications are essential:

A state is relative to a system boundary. The state of a pendulum, the state of a pendulum plus its actuator, and the state of an entire experimental apparatus need not contain the same information.
A state is indexed by time. \(x(t)\) refers to the state assigned at a particular time or sampling instant, not to the system in general.
A state is relative to a description and purpose. A model may omit microscopic details while retaining enough information for the evolution it is intended to describe. Its state is therefore not automatically the complete physical condition of the real system.

Three closely related expressions should not be collapsed:

A state description specifies the chosen collection and structure of future-relevant variables, such as “angle and angular velocity.”
A state value is one realized condition under that description at a particular time, such as a particular angle and angular velocity at \(t\).
A state vector is a coordinate representation of a state value, commonly written \(x(t)\). The same state information may admit another coordinate representation.

Later LDG objects therefore use “possible states” to mean admissible state values, not alternative state descriptions.



For a specified system description, let \(x(t)\) represent its state value at time \(t\). The proposed description qualifies as a state description if the model can continue from \(t\) using:

\(x(t)\);
the specified evolution rule and fixed parameters; and
the future values or prescription of external inputs, where the modeled evolution depends on them,

without separately requiring the system’s history before \(t\).
In a deterministic description, these items specify the modeled future. The state description need not be the smallest possible collection: redundant variables can be included, although minimality may be desirable. Nor is its coordinate representation unique.
LDG generalization: for a probabilistic description, LDG applies the same future-sufficiency criterion to the model’s distribution of possible futures rather than to one exactly determined future. This extension is not attributed here to the deterministic textbook definition cited above.
This is a criterion inside a declared model. Calling \(x(t)\) a state asserts future-relevance and adequacy for that model; it does not establish that \(x(t)\) is a complete or uniquely correct description of the physical system.
Physical condition versus model-defined state. A real system admits descriptions at different scales and with different boundaries. A model-defined state is the information retained for one such description. It can be scientifically useful without being identical to a complete microscopic physical description, but its adequacy must not be claimed beyond the model’s stated scale and assumptions.




\(t\): the time or sampling instant at which the state is defined.
\(x(t)\): the state value at time \(t\); when coordinates are used, its coordinate tuple is the state vector.
\(x_i(t)\): one state variable or coordinate within a multivariable state description.
\(u(t)\): an optional external input, kept conceptually separate from the state.
\(\theta\): fixed parameters of the specified model over the interval being considered.
\(y(t)\): an observation or measurement related to the system at time \(t\).

The letters are conventional, not definitions. A quantity’s role must be stated rather than inferred from its symbol.



Assumed background: basic functions of time and elementary vector notation. No existing LDG Knowledge Object is required.










Concept
Distinction from state




Observation or measurement
An observation is information obtained through a sensor, recording process, or behavioral readout. It may be noisy, partial, delayed, or indirect. A state is defined by its role in continuing the system description. An ideal observation can coincide numerically with the state, but the roles remain distinct: one is what is measured, the other is what the model carries forward. One observation need not reveal the state uniquely, and a measured vector is not automatically a state.


Variable
A variable is a named quantity that can take values. A state is a collection of variable values with a joint future-relevance role. A variable may instead be an observation, input, parameter, or derived summary.


Parameter
A parameter indexes or specifies the model or evolution rule and is held fixed under the declared description; a state value is initialized and propagated by that description. The distinction is about modeling role, not whether a number happens to change: a state may remain constant, for example at equilibrium. An unknown constant parameter can sometimes be incorporated into an augmented state if the description is explicitly reformulated that way.


External input
An external input is a time-varying influence treated as originating outside the chosen system boundary. It can affect future evolution, but its future values are not generally contained in the current internal state. Past input effects that persist must be represented in the current state.


Latent state
A latent state is a state that is not directly observed and is instead inferred or posited by a model. “Latent” concerns access through observations; “state” concerns the variable’s future-relevance role. A hidden variable is not automatically an adequate state, and a latent state need not correspond uniquely to a physical entity.


Description or feature vector
A state description specifies the structure of future-relevant variables; a state value realizes that description at a time. A label, summary statistic, embedding coordinate, or list of contemporaneous features counts as a state description only if it is adequate for the specified evolution question.






Calling something a state does not by itself imply that:

it is directly observable or exactly recoverable from raw measurements;
a single measurement determines it uniquely;
it contains every physical detail of the real system;
it is the only valid state representation or uses unique coordinates;
it is minimal, low-dimensional, noise-free, or continuous;
its future is deterministic;
every component has an independent physical interpretation;
the proposed variables are actually adequate for prediction outside the assumptions and scale of the model; or
fitting or visualizing a time-varying feature vector establishes a dynamical mechanism.




Consider an idealized damped pendulum moving in a plane. Suppose the system boundary includes the pendulum but treats its length and damping coefficient as fixed model parameters and an applied torque as an external input.
At time \(t\), the angle alone is generally not an adequate state: two pendulums can have the same angle while moving in opposite directions, leading to different immediate futures. A standard state description therefore contains both angle and angular velocity,
\[
x(t) = \bigl(\text{angle at }t,\;\text{angular velocity at }t\bigr).
\]
A camera-derived angle estimate is an observation. It may be noisy and does not by itself supply angular velocity. Pendulum length and damping are parameters under this description, while applied torque after \(t\) is an input. If angle and angular velocity are inferred from video rather than directly measured, they are latent relative to that observation process, but they retain the role of state variables in the pendulum model.



In neural population analysis, a common operational description places the activity of each recorded neuron on one coordinate axis, so that the vector of population activity at a time is a point in those coordinates. Cunningham and Yu support this population-coordinate construction and distinguish recorded population activity from lower-dimensional latent variables extracted from it (Cunningham and Yu 2014). Calling that vector an operational recorded-population state is LDG’s framing when a study assigns it the role of state; it is not a claim made by the source and does not show that the vector is the complete state of the circuit, brain, or behaving organism.
The same discipline applies to behavior. A video frame, pose estimate, cursor position, or task label is first an observation or feature. It should be called a behavioral state only relative to a declared system boundary and when its information is adequate for the evolution being studied. Additional variables such as velocity, task context, or unobserved internal condition may be required; which ones matter is an empirical and modeling question.



Later LDG work will compare measured neural and behavioral variables with inferred latent descriptions and their change over time. The concept of state provides the role assignment needed before any such analysis: LDG must say what system is being modeled, at what time scale, which quantities constitute the proposed state, which are observations, which are inputs or parameters, and what claim of future adequacy is being made.
This prevents several recurring errors: treating a data vector as a state merely because it is time-indexed, treating inferred coordinates as uniquely real, or interpreting predictive performance as automatic evidence that the chosen state is physically complete or mechanistically correct.




For a particular neural or behavioral dataset, what evidence would show that a proposed state omits future-relevant information?
At what system boundary and temporal resolution is a proposed state intended to be adequate?
When several state descriptions support similar predictions, what additional evidence should determine which description is scientifically useful?

title: State
text: The state of a specified system at time \(t\) is the current information its chosen description carries forward to determine or predict later evolution.

title: State
text:
State is the point at which a description of a changing system separates relevant past from future evolution. Effects of the past that still matter must be carried in the current state; details of the past that no longer matter need not be retained separately. This makes the term stronger than “what was measured now” and more specific than “a set of variables.”
A clear state definition also assigns different roles to quantities in a model. Some quantities change as part of the system, some are measured from it, some are fixed features of the model, and some influence it from outside the chosen boundary. Confusing these roles makes later claims about dynamics difficult to interpret.

title: State
text:
Imagine pausing a system at time \(t\). A state description is adequate if it contains the information that must be carried forward to continue the description from that time, without consulting the earlier history again. Åström and Murray express this by describing state variables as variables that summarize the past for predicting the future; they also emphasize that choosing how accurately to represent the relevant information is a modeling decision (Åström and Murray 2021, sec. 3.2).
Three qualifications are essential:

A state is relative to a system boundary. The state of a pendulum, the state of a pendulum plus its actuator, and the state of an entire experimental apparatus need not contain the same information.
A state is indexed by time. \(x(t)\) refers to the state assigned at a particular time or sampling instant, not to the system in general.
A state is relative to a description and purpose. A model may omit microscopic details while retaining enough information for the evolution it is intended to describe. Its state is therefore not automatically the complete physical condition of the real system.

Three closely related expressions should not be collapsed:

A state description specifies the chosen collection and structure of future-relevant variables, such as “angle and angular velocity.”
A state value is one realized condition under that description at a particular time, such as a particular angle and angular velocity at \(t\).
A state vector is a coordinate representation of a state value, commonly written \(x(t)\). The same state information may admit another coordinate representation.

Later LDG objects therefore use “possible states” to mean admissible state values, not alternative state descriptions.

title: State
text:
For a specified system description, let \(x(t)\) represent its state value at time \(t\). The proposed description qualifies as a state description if the model can continue from \(t\) using:

\(x(t)\);
the specified evolution rule and fixed parameters; and
the future values or prescription of external inputs, where the modeled evolution depends on them,

without separately requiring the system’s history before \(t\).
In a deterministic description, these items specify the modeled future. The state description need not be the smallest possible collection: redundant variables can be included, although minimality may be desirable. Nor is its coordinate representation unique.
LDG generalization: for a probabilistic description, LDG applies the same future-sufficiency criterion to the model’s distribution of possible futures rather than to one exactly determined future. This extension is not attributed here to the deterministic textbook definition cited above.
This is a criterion inside a declared model. Calling \(x(t)\) a state asserts future-relevance and adequacy for that model; it does not establish that \(x(t)\) is a complete or uniquely correct description of the physical system.
Physical condition versus model-defined state. A real system admits descriptions at different scales and with different boundaries. A model-defined state is the information retained for one such description. It can be scientifically useful without being identical to a complete microscopic physical description, but its adequacy must not be claimed beyond the model’s stated scale and assumptions.

title: State
text:
\(t\): the time or sampling instant at which the state is defined.
\(x(t)\): the state value at time \(t\); when coordinates are used, its coordinate tuple is the state vector.
\(x_i(t)\): one state variable or coordinate within a multivariable state description.
\(u(t)\): an optional external input, kept conceptually separate from the state.
\(\theta\): fixed parameters of the specified model over the interval being considered.
\(y(t)\): an observation or measurement related to the system at time \(t\).

The letters are conventional, not definitions. A quantity’s role must be stated rather than inferred from its symbol.

title: State
text: Assumed background: basic functions of time and elementary vector notation. No existing LDG Knowledge Object is required.

title: State
text:
Concept
Distinction from state




Observation or measurement
An observation is information obtained through a sensor, recording process, or behavioral readout. It may be noisy, partial, delayed, or indirect. A state is defined by its role in continuing the system description. An ideal observation can coincide numerically with the state, but the roles remain distinct: one is what is measured, the other is what the model carries forward. One observation need not reveal the state uniquely, and a measured vector is not automatically a state.


Variable
A variable is a named quantity that can take values. A state is a collection of variable values with a joint future-relevance role. A variable may instead be an observation, input, parameter, or derived summary.


Parameter
A parameter indexes or specifies the model or evolution rule and is held fixed under the declared description; a state value is initialized and propagated by that description. The distinction is about modeling role, not whether a number happens to change: a state may remain constant, for example at equilibrium. An unknown constant parameter can sometimes be incorporated into an augmented state if the description is explicitly reformulated that way.


External input
An external input is a time-varying influence treated as originating outside the chosen system boundary. It can affect future evolution, but its future values are not generally contained in the current internal state. Past input effects that persist must be represented in the current state.


Latent state
A latent state is a state that is not directly observed and is instead inferred or posited by a model. “Latent” concerns access through observations; “state” concerns the variable’s future-relevance role. A hidden variable is not automatically an adequate state, and a latent state need not correspond uniquely to a physical entity.


Description or feature vector
A state description specifies the structure of future-relevant variables; a state value realizes that description at a time. A label, summary statistic, embedding coordinate, or list of contemporaneous features counts as a state description only if it is adequate for the specified evolution question.

title: State
State
text:
Consider an idealized damped pendulum moving in a plane. Suppose the system boundary includes the pendulum but treats its length and damping coefficient as fixed model parameters and an applied torque as an external input.
At time \(t\), the angle alone is generally not an adequate state: two pendulums can have the same angle while moving in opposite directions, leading to different immediate futures. A standard state description therefore contains both angle and angular velocity,
\[
x(t) = \bigl(\text{angle at }t,\;\text{angular velocity at }t\bigr).
\]
A camera-derived angle estimate is an observation. It may be noisy and does not by itself supply angular velocity. Pendulum length and damping are parameters under this description, while applied torque after \(t\) is an input. If angle and angular velocity are inferred from video rather than directly measured, they are latent relative to that observation process, but they retain the role of state variables in the pendulum model.

title: State
text:
In neural population analysis, a common operational description places the activity of each recorded neuron on one coordinate axis, so that the vector of population activity at a time is a point in those coordinates. Cunningham and Yu support this population-coordinate construction and distinguish recorded population activity from lower-dimensional latent variables extracted from it (Cunningham and Yu 2014). Calling that vector an operational recorded-population state is LDG’s framing when a study assigns it the role of state; it is not a claim made by the source and does not show that the vector is the complete state of the circuit, brain, or behaving organism.
The same discipline applies to behavior. A video frame, pose estimate, cursor position, or task label is first an observation or feature. It should be called a behavioral state only relative to a declared system boundary and when its information is adequate for the evolution being studied. Additional variables such as velocity, task context, or unobserved internal condition may be required; which ones matter is an empirical and modeling question.

title: State
text:
Later LDG work will compare measured neural and behavioral variables with inferred latent descriptions and their change over time. The concept of state provides the role assignment needed before any such analysis: LDG must say what system is being modeled, at what time scale, which quantities constitute the proposed state, which are observations, which are inputs or parameters, and what claim of future adequacy is being made.
This prevents several recurring errors: treating a data vector as a state merely because it is time-indexed, treating inferred coordinates as uniquely real, or interpreting predictive performance as automatic evidence that the chosen state is physically complete or mechanistically correct.

title: State
text:

At what system boundary and temporal resolution is a proposed state intended to be adequate?
When several state descriptions support similar predictions, what additional evidence should determine which description is scientifically useful?

These are model- and dataset-specific questions; the L1 definition does not resolve them in advance.

title: State-Space Model
text:
A state-space model specifies both how a state evolves and how observations are generated from that state.



State-space models keep latent evolution, inputs, process uncertainty, and measurement separate while connecting them in one generative description. This makes them central to filtering, smoothing, forecasting, system identification, and latent-dynamics analysis.



One equation moves the hidden state forward; another equation turns the hidden state into data. Inference works backward from observations to uncertain states.



Let \((\mathcal X,\Sigma_{\mathcal X})\) be a state space, \((\mathcal Y,\Sigma_{\mathcal Y})\) an observation space, \((\mathcal U,\Sigma_{\mathcal U})\) an optional input space, and \(\theta=(\theta_0,\theta_x,\theta_y)\) model parameters in declared measurable parameter spaces. A discrete-time probabilistic state-space model specifies an initial law \(\mu_{\theta_0}\), transition kernels \(Q_{k,\theta_x}\), and observation kernels \(G_{k,\theta_y}\). In measure notation,
\[
X_0\sim\mu_{\theta_0},
\]
\[
Q_{k,\theta_x}(x,u,A)
=
\Pr(X_{k+1}\in A\mid X_k=x,u_k=u,\theta_x),
\]
\[
G_{k,\theta_y}(x,u,B)
=
\Pr(Y_k\in B\mid X_k=x,u_k=u,\theta_y),
\]
for measurable \(A\in\Sigma_{\mathcal X}\) and \(B\in\Sigma_{\mathcal Y}\). Here \(\mu_{\theta_0}\) is a probability measure on \(\mathcal X\); for fixed parameters, \(A\mapsto Q_{k,\theta_x}(x,u,A)\) is a probability measure and \((x,u)\mapsto Q_{k,\theta_x}(x,u,A)\) is measurable, with analogous conditions for \(G_{k,\theta_y}\). When parameters vary as kernel arguments, the corresponding joint measurability is required. When suitable dominating measures exist, the same components can be written as densities:

an initial-state law \[
p(x_0\mid\theta_0);
\]
a transition kernel \[
p(x_{k+1}\mid x_k,u_k,\theta_x);
\]
an observation kernel \[
p(y_k\mid x_k,u_k,\theta_y).
\]

Under the explicit assumptions that the latent state is first-order Markov conditional on the input sequence and that observations are conditionally independent given the contemporaneous state, input, and parameters, the generative joint distribution factors as
\[
\begin{aligned}
&p(x_{0:T},y_{0:T}\mid u_{0:T},\theta)\\
&=p(x_0\mid\theta_0)
  \prod_{k=0}^{T-1}p(x_{k+1}\mid x_k,u_k,\theta_x)
  \prod_{k=0}^{T}p(y_k\mid x_k,u_k,\theta_y).
\end{aligned}
\]
If observations do not depend directly on input, omit \(u_k\) from the observation kernel. Higher-order state dependence, correlated observation errors, observation memory, or shared disturbances require a different factorization or an augmented state. The Markov and emission assumptions are modeling choices, not consequences of writing variables with time indices.
The displayed distribution conditions on \(u_{0:T}\) and therefore contains no probability law for the inputs. Random, endogenous, or feedback-generated inputs require an additional input model or an enlarged system boundary.


A deterministic state-space model can be written
\[
x_{k+1}=F_k(x_k,u_k;\theta_x),
\qquad
y_k=G_k(x_k,u_k;\theta_y).
\]
When \(F_k\) and \(G_k\) are measurable, these equations correspond to Dirac transition and observation kernels concentrated at \(F_k(x_k,u_k;\theta_x)\) and \(G_k(x_k,u_k;\theta_y)\).
An additive stochastic special case is
\[
x_{k+1}=F_k(x_k,u_k;\theta_x)+w_k,
\qquad
y_k=G_k(x_k,u_k;\theta_y)+v_k.
\]
Here \(w_k\) enters state evolution and \(v_k\) enters observation generation. Their distributions, dependence, correlation across time, mutual independence, and independence from the initial state are separate assumptions. An uncertain initial state \(x_0\sim p(x_0\mid\theta_0)\) is not process noise: it is uncertainty before the first modeled transition.



A continuous-time model may specify
\[
\dot x(t)=f(t,x(t),u(t);\theta_x)
\]
or a stochastic differential/state process, together with observations at times \(t_k\),
\[
y_k\sim p(y_k\mid x(t_k),u(t_k),\theta_y).
\]
When the continuous state process is well posed, it induces finite-time transition kernels \(Q^{\theta_x}_{s,t}\) between sampling times. A deterministic evolution induces a Dirac kernel. Stochastic transition laws may be available only implicitly or numerically; not every continuous stochastic model has a simple transition density. Continuous-discrete models must therefore state the state process, observation schedule, and approximation used for any discrete transition likelihood.



The state-space model is the forward generative specification above. It is distinct from algorithms or target distributions used for:

filtering: \(p(x_k\mid y_{0:k},u_{0:k})\);
smoothing: \(p(x_{0:T}\mid y_{0:T},u_{0:T})\);
prediction/forecasting: future states or observations conditional on available data;
parameter learning/system identification: estimating \(\theta\) or model structure.

Observability asks whether state information can be recovered from outputs under a transition model. Identifiability asks whether different full model specifications induce different observable distributions. Neither property follows merely from writing a state-space model.





\(x_k\): latent or observed state.
\(u_k\): optional input.
\(y_k\): observation.
\(F_k\) or \(p(x_{k+1}\mid x_k,u_k,\theta_x)\): deterministic or probabilistic transition model.
\(G_k\) or \(p(y_k\mid x_k,u_k,\theta_y)\): deterministic or probabilistic observation model.
\(\mu_{\theta_0},Q_{k,\theta_x},G_{k,\theta_y}\): initial law, transition kernel, and observation kernel.
\(p(x_0\mid\theta_0)\): initial-state law.
\(w_k\), \(v_k\): process and observation disturbances.
\(\theta_0,\theta_x,\theta_y\): initial, transition, and observation parameters.




State Space defines admissible states. Observation Model defines the measurement relation. Input-Driven Dynamics supplies input-conditioned transition language.
Process Noise and Observation Noise distinguish the two stochastic locations used in common special cases.










Concept
Distinction




Dynamical system
May specify state evolution without any observation equation.


Observation model
Only the measurement component of a state-space model.


Linear dynamical system
Often refers to linear state evolution, even when no observation equation is specified. A linear state-space model additionally requires the included observation relation to be linear.


Hidden Markov model
A state-space model with a Markov latent process, often discrete-valued; terminology varies.


Filter / smoother
An inference procedure or posterior target based on a state-space model, not the generative model itself.


Observability
A recoverability property of transition and observation structure across time, not guaranteed by the model format.


Identifiability
A uniqueness property of the induced observable distribution, not guaranteed by state-space notation.


Initial-state uncertainty
Uncertainty in \(x_0\) before the first transition; it is distinct from process disturbances injected at later steps.






A state-space model does not imply linearity, Gaussianity, low-dimensional state, time homogeneity, conditional independence beyond what is stated, observability, identifiability, tractable inference, or that inferred state equals physical ground truth. Good filtering or forecasting performance does not validate the state variables as a unique mechanism.



Consider
\[
x_0\sim\mathcal N(0,P_0),
\]
\[
x_{k+1}=0.9x_k+w_k,
\qquad
w_k\sim\mathcal N(0,Q),
\]
\[
y_k=x_k+v_k,
\qquad
v_k\sim\mathcal N(0,R).
\]
If \(x_0\), \((w_k)\), and \((v_k)\) are mutually independent and each noise sequence is independent across time, the model has the standard Markov/emission factorization. \(P_0\) describes initial uncertainty, \(Q\) transition uncertainty, and \(R\) measurement uncertainty. Moving \(v_k\) into the state equation or \(w_k\) into the observation equation changes the model’s scientific meaning.
A filter can estimate \(p(x_k\mid y_{0:k})\), but that estimate and the algorithm producing it are not additional parts of the state-space model definition.



State-space models can represent latent neural trajectories with spiking or continuous observations and external task inputs. Their usefulness depends on testing transition and observation assumptions separately.



At L2, this object joins the dynamics and latent-variable branches through an explicit initial law, transition model, observation model, and conditional factorization. It keeps the generative specification separate from inference algorithms and from claims of observability, identifiability, or mechanism.




Which state dimension and transition family are justified?
How should irregular sampling enter the model?
What baselines reveal whether dynamics improve over independent latent factors?





Åström and Murray give the inspected deterministic state-dynamics/output formulation and a linear-Gaussian uncertain-initial-state/two-noise special case (Åström and Murray 2021, secs. 3.2, 8.4).
Kalman provides an inspected primary linear stochastic state-transition, random-excitation, partial-observation, and filtering framework while treating model construction and estimation as separate problems (Kalman 1960). His inspected formulation is not cited here as the source of a separate additive measurement-noise term.
Filtering, smoothing, forecasting, parameter estimation, observability tests, and identifiability theorems are intentionally deferred.





Contains distinct transition and observation components.
Allows inputs and two noise locations.
States linearity and identifiability non-implications.
Types the initial-state law, transition kernel, and observation kernel.
States Markov and conditional-emission assumptions before factorizing the joint distribution.
Separates initial uncertainty, process noise, and observation noise.
Relates continuous-time state evolution to sampled observations without assuming a closed-form density.
Separates the generative model from filtering, smoothing, forecasting, learning, observability, and identifiability.

title: Riemannian Metric
text:
A Riemannian metric assigns a positive-definite inner product to every tangent space of a smooth manifold, varying smoothly from point to point.



A smooth manifold supplies local coordinates but no canonical lengths or angles. A Riemannian metric adds the structure needed to measure tangent vectors, curve length, angle, volume, geodesic distance, and curvature.



At each point, place a smoothly changing ruler and protractor on the tangent space. The rulers may stretch different directions by different amounts.



Let \(M\) be a smooth \(n\)-manifold. A Riemannian metric is a smooth symmetric positive-definite covariant \(2\)-tensor field
\[
g\in\Gamma(S^2T^*M).
\]
Equivalently, each \(p\in M\) receives an inner product
\[
g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R
\]
such that \(p\mapsto g_p(X_p,Y_p)\) is smooth for smooth vector fields \(X,Y\). Symmetry and positive definiteness mean
\[
g_p(v,w)=g_p(w,v),
\qquad
g_p(v,v)>0\quad(v\ne0).
\]
Lee gives this definition and its elementary constructions (Lee 1997, ch. 3).


In coordinates \(x=(x^1,\ldots,x^n)\),
\[
g=g_{ij}(x)\,dx^i\otimes dx^j,
\]
where \([g_{ij}(x)]\) is a smooth symmetric positive-definite matrix. Under coordinates \(y=y(x)\),
\[
g'_{ab}(y)
=
\frac{\partial x^i}{\partial y^a}
\frac{\partial x^j}{\partial y^b}
g_{ij}(x(y)).
\]
Thus the component matrix changes by the tensor transformation law; the geometric metric does not equal one fixed matrix independent of coordinates.



For \(v,w\in T_pM\),
\[
\|v\|_{g,p}=\sqrt{g_p(v,v)},
\]
and for nonzero vectors
\[
\cos\angle_g(v,w)
=
\frac{g_p(v,w)}{\|v\|_{g,p}\|w\|_{g,p}}.
\]
Orthogonality means \(g_p(v,w)=0\). These quantities compare vectors in the same tangent space; comparing vectors at different points requires additional transport or coordinates.



For a piecewise smooth curve \(\gamma:[a,b]\to M\),
\[
L_g(\gamma)
=
\int_a^b
\sqrt{g_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t),\dot\gamma(t))}
\,dt.
\]
This length is invariant under orientation-preserving reparameterizations. On a connected component, the induced Riemannian distance is
\[
d_g(p,q)
=
\inf_{\gamma:p\to q}L_g(\gamma),
\]
where the infimum ranges over piecewise smooth curves joining \(p\) and \(q\). Lee shows that this is a metric on a connected Riemannian manifold (Lee 1997, ch. 6). Points in distinct connected components have no joining curve; one either treats distance componentwise or uses an extended distance \(+\infty\).
The infimum need not initially be attained, and the existence or uniqueness of a minimizing geodesic requires additional conditions. The Geodesic object records the local relationship without assuming global minimizers.



For a smooth map \(F:M\to N\) and a Riemannian metric \(h\) on \(N\), the pullback tensor is
\[
(F^*h)_p(v,w)
=
h_{F(p)}(dF_pv,dF_pw).
\]
It is symmetric and nonnegative. It is positive definite—and hence a Riemannian metric on \(M\)—when \(dF_p\) is injective for every \(p\), for example when \(F\) is an immersion. For an embedded submanifold, the inclusion pulls the ambient metric back to the standard induced metric (Lee 1997, ch. 3). An arbitrary non-injective map can yield a degenerate pullback and does not automatically define a Riemannian metric.
A diffeomorphism \(F:(M,g)\to(N,h)\) is an isometry when \(F^*h=g\). Isometric descriptions preserve the Riemannian lengths, angles, and induced distances even though coordinate matrices may differ.





\(g\): Riemannian metric.
\(g_p(v,w)=\langle v,w\rangle_p\): inner product at \(p\).
\(\|v\|_p=\sqrt{g_p(v,v)}\): tangent-vector norm.
\(L_g(\gamma)\): curve length induced by \(g\).
\(d_g(p,q)\): point distance obtained as an infimum of curve lengths.
\(g_{ij}\): coordinate matrix of metric components.
\(F^*h\): pullback metric/tensor.
\(dF_p\): differential used to test pullback nondegeneracy.




Metric supplies distance language. Tangent Space supplies the vector spaces receiving inner products.










Concept
Distinction




Metric-space metric
Directly assigns point-to-point distance; a Riemannian metric first acts on tangent vectors and induces distance through path lengths.


Euclidean metric
A constant special case in Euclidean coordinates.


Mahalanobis distance
A fixed positive-definite quadratic metric on a vector space, corresponding to a constant Riemannian metric in those coordinates; semidefinite matrices yield only pseudodistance.


Pseudo-Riemannian metric
Uses a nondegenerate but indefinite bilinear form and need not define ordinary positive distance.


Sub-Riemannian metric
Defines inner products only on a selected tangent distribution; admissible path length and distance require additional bracket/accessibility structure.


Finsler metric
Uses a smoothly varying norm that need not arise from a quadratic inner product.


Learned metric
A fitted local or global distance/tensor model whose positivity, smoothness, identifiability, and generalization require validation.






A Riemannian metric does not imply zero curvature, completeness, unique coordinates, a unique data-derived choice, global geodesic existence or uniqueness, an isometric embedding in a chosen ambient space, or biological meaning. Positive-definite fitted matrices at sampled points do not by themselves establish a smooth global metric field.



On \(\mathbb R^2\), the Euclidean metric is
\[
g=dx^2+dy^2.
\]
If \(a(x,y)>0\) is smooth, the position-dependent metric \(g=a(x,y)^2dx^2+dy^2\) assigns different local costs to motion in the \(x\) direction.



A learned local metric can encode anisotropic variability or task sensitivity in latent space. It must be evaluated against simpler fixed metrics and should not be interpreted mechanistically from fit alone.



At L2, Riemannian Metric supplies typed coordinate transformations, tangent norms/angles, curve lengths, induced distance, pullback conditions, and isometry language needed for geodesics and curvature without conflating nonlinear embeddings with geometry.

How should metric uncertainty be represented?
When does a learned metric improve prediction beyond Euclidean or covariance baselines?

Connection, volume, completion, geodesic-existence, embedding, and metric-learning proofs are intentionally deferred.

title: Phase Space
text:
A phase space is the state space used to represent a dynamical system so that each point denotes one admissible instantaneous state and each trajectory traces the system’s evolution through those states.



The term emphasizes a dynamical reading of a state space: points are possible system states, while curves through the space are trajectories generated or considered over time. It is especially common when position-like and velocity- or momentum-like variables must be represented together.
LDG keeps “phase space” and “state space” close but not automatically identical. Some fields use them interchangeably; others reserve phase space for a particular dynamical construction. A reader should therefore inspect the declared variables and system boundary rather than infer them from the label alone.



A photograph of a pendulum angle cannot distinguish motion to the left from motion to the right. A phase-space description using angle and angular velocity assigns those cases different points. As time passes, the point moves and draws a trajectory.



Let \(\mathcal{X}\) be the admissible state values for a specified dynamical description and let \(x:I\to\mathcal{X}\) be a trajectory. Calling \(\mathcal{X}\) the phase space highlights the pair:

each \(x\in\mathcal{X}\) is one instantaneous state value; and
system evolution is represented by trajectories or a flow acting on \(\mathcal{X}\).

For a second-order scalar equation, a common first-order state is \(x=(q,v)\) with \(v=\dot q\), so the corresponding phase space may be a subset of pairs \((q,v)\). Teschl uses this convention for Newtonian systems (Teschl 2012, sec. 6.7).
This definition does not require Euclidean coordinates globally. A phase space may be an abstract set with additional structure, a Euclidean domain, or—when separately justified—a smooth manifold. Calling a representation a phase space does not supply that additional structure by itself.


For a finite-dimensional second-order system, let \(q(t),v(t)\in\mathbb R^n\) and let \(F:U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\). Starting from
\[
\ddot q=F(q,\dot q),
\]
introduce the velocity variable \(v=\dot q\) and phase coordinate \(x=(q,v)\in U\). The system becomes
\[
\dot x
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\dot q\\
\dot v
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
v\\
F(q,v)
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
This construction explains the common position–velocity convention: one phase point contains the information required by the first-order evolution rule (Teschl 2012, sec. 1.1). It does not prove existence, uniqueness, completeness, or the adequacy of \((q,v)\) as a real-system state, and it does not imply that every scientific state description has position and velocity components.






TipLDG Synthesis



For a smooth configuration manifold \(Q\), velocity-state descriptions are naturally represented using the tangent bundle \(TQ\). Hamiltonian formulations instead commonly replace velocity by momentum and use position–momentum coordinates, with cotangent-bundle language supplying the intrinsic generalization (Teschl 2012, sec. 8.3; Mrowka 2004). Relating \(TQ\) and \(T^*Q\) requires additional mechanical structure, so LDG does not treat either convention as the universal meaning of phase space.





Let \(h:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y\) be a time-independent diffeomorphism and set \(y(t)=h(x(t))\). If
\[
\dot x=f(x),
\]
then the coordinate expression in \(y\) is
\[
\dot y
=
Dh(x)f(x)
=
Dh\bigl(h^{-1}(y)\bigr)f\bigl(h^{-1}(y)\bigr).
\]
Thus numerical coordinates, vector components, and the appearance of a phase portrait can change while representing the same abstract states and trajectories. A time-dependent coordinate transformation would contribute an additional partial-time derivative and is outside this bounded formula. A projection or non-injective observation map can collapse distinct phase points and need not preserve the dynamics.



LDG convention: a phase portrait is a coordinate-dependent representation of selected trajectories, orbits, vector-field directions, invariant sets, or other qualitative features in phase space. Teschl directly uses phase portraits as collections of plotted solution structure for autonomous systems (Teschl 2012, secs. 3.2, 6.7). The broader LDG convention makes explicit which additional qualitative overlays are being shown. A portrait is evidence about the specified model or fitted representation, not a proof that recorded data constitute the complete phase space.





\(\mathcal{X}\): the phase space or dynamical state space.
\(x\in\mathcal{X}\): one phase point, meaning one state value.
\(x(t)\): the phase point occupied at time \(t\).
\(x:I\to\mathcal{X}\): one trajectory.
\((q,v)\): a common position–velocity coordinate pair.
\(f(x)\): coordinate expression of a first-order vector field.
\(h:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y\): time-independent diffeomorphic coordinate change.
\(Dh(x)\): derivative/Jacobian transporting vector components between coordinates.
\(TQ\): velocity phase space associated with a smooth configuration manifold \(Q\), when that manifold structure is independently justified.




State Space defines admissible state values. Trajectory supplies the time-indexed path through those values.
Assumed background: elementary derivatives, Jacobians, coordinate pairs, and first-order rewriting of a second-order equation. Tangent-bundle derivations are deferred to dedicated geometry objects.










Concept
Relationship




State space
The broader LDG term for admissible states under a specified description. “Phase space” emphasizes that those states are being used for dynamics; usage conventions vary.


Phase portrait
A drawing or collection of trajectories in chosen phase-space coordinates. The portrait is a representation, not the phase space itself.


Trajectory
One time-parameterized evolution in the phase space, not the collection of all admissible states.


Orbit
The visited-state set of a trajectory after time labels are discarded. A phase portrait may show orbits without preserving timing.


Observation space
Values produced by a measurement model. An observation vector need not identify a phase point uniquely.


Embedding
A representation map into an ambient space. The embedded image is distinct from the intrinsic source object, but a verified structure-preserving embedding with pushed-forward dynamics can provide an equivalent realization. A generic dimensionality-reduction map need not be injective or dynamics-preserving.


Manifold
A possible smooth structure for a phase space when separately established. “Phase space” alone does not imply a manifold.






Calling a set a phase space does not imply that:

plotted data have been shown to be the true state of the system;
the space is low-dimensional, Euclidean, smooth, or a manifold;
a two-dimensional visualization preserves the system’s dynamics;
temporal samples define a vector field or flow;
the chosen coordinates are unique or mechanistically privileged; or
nearby plotted points are close under a scientifically meaningful metric.
a phase portrait preserves elapsed time, density, uncertainty, or unobserved state variables; or
an invertible coordinate convention has been established for a learned projection.




For \(\ddot q=-q\), set \(x=(q,v)\) with \(v=\dot q\). The phase space is \(\mathbb{R}^2\) in these coordinates, and trajectories satisfy
\[
\dot q=v,\qquad \dot v=-q.
\]
Each point gives both position and velocity. Circular trajectories in this example are consequences of the specified equation, not evidence that every phase space is circular or two-dimensional.



A neural or behavioral phase-space plot may place selected activity variables, latent coordinates, positions, or velocities on axes. Such a plot becomes a phase-space representation only relative to an explicit state description. A delay embedding or low-dimensional projection is not automatically the system’s state space.



At L2, Phase Space gives LDG a typed bridge from higher-order equations to first-order dynamics and clarifies how coordinate transformations alter formulas and portraits without necessarily altering the underlying evolution. It also enforces a boundary: visualizing neural activity in coordinates is not by itself evidence for a manifold, an invertible embedding, or a complete state description.




When should LDG use “phase space” rather than the more general “state space”?
Which measured or inferred variables are sufficient to form a useful phase-space description?
How should uncertainty in an inferred phase point be represented?





Teschl provides the inspected first-order position–velocity reduction, trajectory/orbit terminology, and dynamical-systems convention (Teschl 2012, secs. 1.1, 6.2–6.3, 6.7).
Teschl provides inspected phase-portrait examples and first-order autonomous-system context (Teschl 2012, secs. 3.2, 6.7).
Mrowka provides the inspected chart and coordinate-change framework used only to delimit the manifold case (Mrowka 2004, secs. 1, 7.2).





Defines phase space through states and trajectories.
Distinguishes phase space, state space, phase portrait, and observation space.
Includes a minimal first-order mechanical example.
States that a visualization or embedding does not establish manifold structure.
Rewrites a bounded second-order system as a typed first-order phase-space system.
States how vector-field coordinates transform under a time-independent diffeomorphism.
Separates phase point, trajectory, orbit, portrait, observation, embedding, and manifold roles.

title: Observation Model
text:
An observation model specifies how latent or system variables are related probabilistically or deterministically to the measurements available to an analyst.



The observation model separates what a system is modeled as doing from how that activity becomes data. Without this separation, measurement distortion, subsampling, and noise can be mistaken for latent dynamics.



The latent quantity is what the model posits; the observation model is the measurement channel. Two experiments can observe the same latent process through different sensors and therefore produce different data.



Let \((\mathcal Z,\Sigma_{\mathcal Z})\) be a latent or state space, \((\mathcal Y,\Sigma_{\mathcal Y})\) an observation space, and \((\Theta_y,\Sigma_{\Theta_y})\) an observation-parameter space.
A deterministic observation model is a measurable map
\[
y=g(z;\theta_y),
\qquad
g:\mathcal Z\times\Theta_y\to\mathcal Y.
\]
A probabilistic observation model is a conditional probability law
\[
p(y\mid z,\theta_y),
\]
or, more generally, a probability kernel
\[
K_{\theta_y}(z,A)
=
\Pr(Y\in A\mid Z=z,\theta_y),
\qquad A\in\Sigma_{\mathcal Y},
\]
assigning an observation distribution to each \((z,\theta_y)\). For each fixed \(\theta_y\) and \(z\), the map \(A\mapsto K_{\theta_y}(z,A)\) is a probability measure; for each \(A\in\Sigma_{\mathcal Y}\), the map \(z\mapsto K_{\theta_y}(z,A)\) is measurable. If \(\theta_y\) varies as part of the kernel argument, joint measurability in \((z,\theta_y)\) is required. Density notation \(p(y\mid z,\theta_y)\) requires a suitable dominating measure; the kernel formulation does not. This is a forward model from latent/state variables to possible observations. It does not by itself specify how to infer \(z\) from \(y\).
For a realized observation \(y\), the conditional density can be viewed as a likelihood in \((z,\theta_y)\),
\[
\mathcal L(z,\theta_y;y)=p(y\mid z,\theta_y),
\]
but a posterior such as \(p(z\mid y)\) additionally requires a latent prior or state model and Bayes’s rule. Tipping and Bishop explicitly distinguish the conditional observation distribution, the marginal observation distribution obtained by integrating out the latent variable, and the conditional latent distribution used for inference (Tipping and Bishop 1999, sec. 3.1).


For observations \(y_{1:T}\) associated with latent variables \(z_{1:T}\), the factorization
\[
p(y_{1:T}\mid z_{1:T},\theta_y)
=
\prod_{t=1}^{T}p(y_t\mid z_t,\theta_y)
\]
holds only when observations are conditionally independent across time given the corresponding latent variables and parameters. Likewise, a channel factorization
\[
p(y_t\mid z_t,\theta_y)
=
\prod_{j=1}^{D}p(y_{tj}\mid z_t,\theta_y)
\]
requires conditional independence across channels; channel-specific parameter blocks may be used only when that partition of \(\theta_y\) is declared. Correlated sensor errors, temporal filtering, shared observation noise, or history-dependent measurement processes require a joint observation model instead. Tipping and Bishop’s factor-analysis discussion makes conditional independence a consequence of a diagonal error-covariance assumption, not a universal property (Tipping and Bishop 1999, sec. 2.1).



An additive-noise model
\[
y=g(z;\theta_y)+v,
\qquad
v\mid z,\theta_y\sim p_v(\,\cdot\mid z,\theta_y),
\]
induces \(p(y\mid z,\theta_y)\) through the conditional distribution of \(v\). The common fixed-noise-law special case additionally assumes \(v\perp z\mid\theta_y\). Additivity, independence, Gaussianity, homoscedasticity, and zero bias are extra assumptions. Observation noise enters the measurement relation; process noise enters state evolution. Preprocessing artifacts, calibration error, censoring, missingness, and model misspecification are not automatically represented by \(v\).



A deterministic map \(g\) is invertible on its image only when the relevant restriction is one-to-one and has an appropriate inverse. A many-to-one map can make distinct latent values observationally indistinguishable. In probabilistic models, overlapping conditional distributions can likewise limit information about \(z\). These are properties of the forward model; observability additionally uses observations across time and a transition model, while identifiability asks whether model specifications induce distinct observable distributions.



Let \(z'=h(z)\) be a bimeasurable bijective change of latent coordinates. The same deterministic observation relation is represented by
\[
g'(z';\theta_y)=g(h^{-1}(z');\theta_y),
\]
and the same probabilistic kernel by
\[
K'_{\theta_y}(z',A)
=
K_{\theta_y}(h^{-1}(z'),A),
\]
or, when conditional densities exist,
\[
p'(y\mid z',\theta_y)
=
p(y\mid h^{-1}(z'),\theta_y).
\]
To preserve the marginal observable distribution, the latent law must also be pushed forward consistently, \(P_{Z'}=h_\#P_Z\). For a \(C^1\) diffeomorphism between Euclidean coordinate domains, the transformed latent density is
\[
p_{Z'}(z')
=
p_Z(h^{-1}(z'))
\left|\det Dh^{-1}(z')\right|.
\] No latent-coordinate Jacobian is inserted into \(p(y\mid z')\) itself because that density is still taken with respect to the observation variable \(y\). Changing latent coordinates without transforming the observation model and latent law generally defines a different generative model.





\(z\): latent variable or latent state.
\(y\): observation.
\(\mathcal Z,\mathcal Y\): latent/state and observation spaces.
\(g\) or \(W\): deterministic observation mapping.
\(\theta_y\): observation-model parameters.
\(v\) or \(\varepsilon\): observation noise.
\(p(y\mid z,\theta_y)\): conditional forward model or likelihood for observed \(y\).
\(K_{\theta_y}(z,A)\): probability-kernel form of the forward model.
\(p(z\mid y)\): posterior inference quantity requiring additional prior/model assumptions.
\(h\): bijective latent-coordinate reparameterization.




Latent Variable defines the unobserved quantity being related to data.










Concept
Distinction




Dynamics / transition model
Describes how state changes; the observation model describes how state produces measurements.


Decoder
Predicts a target or latent summary from data. It need not be the generative forward measurement relation or its inverse.


Inference model / posterior
Maps observations to uncertainty about latent variables and requires prior or state-model assumptions beyond \(p(y\mid z)\).


Observability
Uses a transition model and observations over time to ask whether state can be recovered; it is not a property of one observation map alone.


Identifiability
Asks whether distinct model specifications imply distinct observable distributions; an explicit observation model is necessary but not sufficient.


Observation noise
One stochastic component of an observation model, not the whole mapping.


Process noise
Perturbs state evolution rather than the conditional measurement relation.


Preprocessing / calibration
Operations and uncertainties applied to recorded data or sensors; they must be modeled explicitly rather than silently labeled observation noise.


Sensor
A physical device; the observation model is a mathematical description of its relevant relation to variables.






An observation model does not imply that the latent variable is identifiable, the mapping is invertible, noise is independent, measurements are unbiased, or a good reconstruction establishes mechanism. Nor does it imply conditional independence across times or channels, observability from a time series, a unique posterior, calibrated uncertainty, or preservation of latent geometry in observation space.



In probabilistic PCA,
\[
z\sim\mathcal N(0,I),
\qquad
y=Wz+\mu+\varepsilon,
\qquad
\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2I),
\qquad
\varepsilon\perp z,
\]
so
\[
p(y\mid z)=\mathcal N(Wz+\mu,\sigma^2I).
\]
The isotropic covariance makes observation channels conditionally independent in the chosen coordinate system; a non-diagonal covariance in those declared channel coordinates would prevent this product factorization. Inferring \(p(z\mid y)\) additionally uses the latent prior \(p(z)\) (Tipping and Bishop 1999, secs. 2.1, 3.1).
For a deterministic information-loss example, \(y=z^2\) cannot distinguish \(z\) from \(-z\). Accurate forward prediction of \(y\) therefore does not make the latent coordinate uniquely recoverable.



Spike counts, fluorescence, EEG sensors, eye position, and behavioral labels are observation channels with different sampling and distortion. Analyses should not transfer geometric or dynamical properties from data space to latent space without checking the observation model.



At L2, Observation Model anchors a typed forward relation between latent/state variables and data, states when likelihood factorizations are valid, and separates information loss from inference, observability, and identifiability. It prepares explicit treatment of observation noise without confusing the measurement channel with dynamics.

When is a nonlinear mapping necessary?
How sensitive are latent conclusions to alternative observation models?

Estimation algorithms, posterior approximations, observability tests, and identifiability theorems are intentionally deferred.

Separates forward likelihood from posterior inference.
Conditions temporal and channel factorization on explicit independence assumptions.

title: Manifold
text:
A smooth manifold is a space that is locally described by Euclidean coordinates whose overlapping coordinate systems change smoothly.



Manifolds allow globally curved or topologically nontrivial spaces to support local calculus. They provide one possible model for latent state spaces, but finite data or a nonlinear visualization does not establish that model.



The surface of a sphere cannot be covered by one undistorted planar coordinate system, yet every sufficiently small patch looks like an open patch of \(\mathbb R^2\). Compatible patches form an atlas.



An \(n\)-dimensional smooth manifold \(M\) is a Hausdorff, second-countable topological space equipped with an atlas of charts \((U_\alpha,\varphi_\alpha)\) whose domains cover \(M\), where
\[
\varphi_\alpha:U_\alpha\to\varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha)\subseteq\mathbb R^n
\]
is a homeomorphism onto an open subset of \(\mathbb R^n\), and the transition maps between overlapping charts are smooth. Mrowka gives this chart-and-atlas definition (Mrowka 2004, sec. 1).
This is an intrinsic definition: a manifold need not first be given as a subset of Euclidean space. An embedding is one way to represent it in an ambient space.




\(M\): manifold.
\(n=\dim M\): manifold dimension.
\((U,\varphi)\): coordinate chart.
\(\varphi(p)\in\mathbb R^n\): local coordinates of \(p\).
\(\varphi_\beta\circ\varphi_\alpha^{-1}\): transition map.




Embedding distinguishes an intrinsic space from one representation of it. Intrinsic Dimension provides the local coordinate count under the manifold model.
Assumed background: open sets, continuity, and elementary topology; the dedicated Topology Concept appears later in the spine.










Concept
Distinction




Linear subspace
Globally closed under linear combinations; a manifold may be curved and only locally Euclidean.


Embedded manifold
A manifold represented as a suitably regular subset of an ambient space.


Point cloud
Finite samples do not themselves supply charts, topology, or smooth transitions.


Topology
Supplies continuity and neighborhood structure; a smooth manifold additionally has compatible differentiable charts.






A manifold claim does not imply a Riemannian metric, known topology, low curvature, global Euclidean coordinates, unique dimension estimate, faithful sampling, or biological mechanism.



The circle \(S^1\) is a one-dimensional manifold. It requires more than one ordinary real-valued chart, although it can be embedded in \(\mathbb R^2\).



Neural or behavioral states may be modeled as lying near a manifold. Such a claim requires evidence beyond dimensionality reduction: local coordinate consistency, scale analysis, sampling adequacy, and comparison with simpler subspaces.



Manifold establishes the object on which tangent spaces, Riemannian metrics, geodesics, and intrinsic curvature can later be defined.




Which data can distinguish a manifold from condition-specific subspaces?
At what scales are chart assumptions defensible?
How should noise away from a candidate manifold be modeled?

Whitney supplies classical embedding context (Whitney 1936).

title: Linear Dynamical System
text:
A linear dynamical system has state evolution that is linear in the state and declared inputs, optionally paired with a linear observation model.



Linear systems are interpretable baselines with tractable propagation and solution structure; exact probabilistic inference requires additional assumptions such as Gaussian noise. They can be exact models or local approximations, but linearity is a structural assumption—not a synonym for low dimension or simplicity in observed behavior.



For a linear system, weighted sums of zero-input solutions remain solutions. Matrices specify how state components interact and how inputs enter.



For \(x(t)\in\mathbb R^n\), \(u(t)\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(y(t)\in\mathbb R^q\), a continuous-time linear time-invariant state-space model has the form
\[
\dot x(t)=Ax(t)+Bu(t),
\qquad
y(t)=Cx(t)+Du(t),
\]
with
\[
A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n},\quad
B\in\mathbb R^{n\times m},\quad
C\in\mathbb R^{q\times n},\quad
D\in\mathbb R^{q\times m}.
\]
A discrete-time counterpart is
\[
x_{k+1}=Ax_k+Bu_k,
\qquad
y_k=Cx_k+Du_k.
\]
The state evolution alone, \(\dot x=Ax+Bu\) or \(x_{k+1}=Ax_k+Bu_k\), is often called a linear dynamical system even when no observation equation is included. A linear state-space model additionally declares the linear observation relation. Åström and Murray use these forms and explicitly separate state, input, and output roles (Åström and Murray 2021, secs. 3.2, 6.1).


For the homogeneous system \(\dot x=Ax\), linear combinations of solutions are solutions. For the input-driven system, the complete response is jointly linear in the initial state and input:
\[
x(t;\alpha x_{0,1}+\beta x_{0,2},\delta u_1+\gamma u_2)
=
\alpha x(t;x_{0,1},0)+\beta x(t;x_{0,2},0)
+
\delta x(t;0,u_1)+\gamma x(t;0,u_2),
\]
with corresponding linearity of the output, when the same matrices, parameters, time origin, admissible input class, and zero affine offsets are used. Superposition does not combine responses from different systems or parameter settings. This separates the homogeneous initial-condition response from the forced zero-initial-state response (Åström and Murray 2021, sec. 6.1).
An offset model
\[
\dot x=Ax+Bu+c,
\qquad
y=Cx+Du+d
\]
is affine, not linear, because it does not preserve zero or arbitrary linear combinations. Translating to deviation coordinates around an operating point or augmenting coordinates with a constant component can produce a linear representation, but both change the representation and must be stated explicitly.



For constant \(A\) and an admissible input, the solution from time \(t_0\) is
\[
x(t)
=
e^{A(t-t_0)}x(t_0)
+
\int_{t_0}^{t}e^{A(t-s)}Bu(s)\,ds.
\]
The first term is the initial-condition response and the integral is the forced response. The output is
\[
y(t)
=
Ce^{A(t-t_0)}x(t_0)
+
\int_{t_0}^{t}Ce^{A(t-s)}Bu(s)\,ds
+
Du(t).
\]
These formulas require constant \(A\); time-varying linear systems use a state-transition operator rather than simply \(e^{A(t-t_0)}\) (Åström and Murray 2021, secs. 6.2–6.3).
The \(D u(t)\) term is direct feedthrough. In an impulse-response representation it must be kept separate from an ordinary function-valued convolution kernel, or represented using a generalized impulse term.



For \(k>j\),
\[
x_k
=
A^{k-j}x_j
+
\sum_{r=j}^{k-1}A^{k-1-r}Bu_r.
\]
Again, the first term propagates the initial state and the sum accumulates input effects. This formula does not imply stability: powers \(A^n\) can decay, remain bounded, or grow depending on \(A\).



Let \(z=Tx\) for an invertible matrix \(T\), while input and output coordinates are left unchanged. The same state evolution in \(z\) coordinates has
\[
A'=TAT^{-1},
\qquad
B'=TB,
\qquad
C'=CT^{-1},
\qquad
D'=D.
\]
For an affine state offset, \(c'=Tc\). If input or output bases are also changed, the formulas for \(B,C,D\) change accordingly. Thus similar dynamics matrices can represent the same abstract linear evolution in different state coordinates. Eigenvalues are preserved by similarity, but state axes, matrix entries, loadings, and component interpretations are not unique or automatically mechanistic.



For a nonlinear model \(\dot x=f(x,u)\), first choose an equilibrium operating point satisfying \(f(x_e,u_e)=0\) and define
\[
\delta x=x-x_e,
\qquad
\delta u=u-u_e,
\qquad
\delta y=y-h(x_e,u_e).
\]
Then define
\[
A=\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right|_{(x_e,u_e)},
\qquad
B=\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial u}\right|_{(x_e,u_e)}.
\]
The residual-free first-order deviation model is
\[
\delta\dot x
\approx
A\,\delta x+B\,\delta u.
\]
If \(y=h(x,u)\), define
\[
C=\left.\frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\right|_{(x_e,u_e)},
\qquad
D=\left.\frac{\partial h}{\partial u}\right|_{(x_e,u_e)},
\]
so \(\delta y\approx C\delta x+D\delta u\). Around a non-equilibrium nominal trajectory \((\bar x(t),\bar u(t))\) satisfying \(\dot{\bar x}(t)=f(\bar x(t),\bar u(t))\), the deviation Jacobians are evaluated along that trajectory and generally vary with time, yielding a linear time-varying approximation. At an arbitrary point that is not an equilibrium or nominal solution, a nonzero residual term remains. This is a local approximation whose accuracy depends on neighborhood and neglected higher-order terms. Successful local linear prediction does not establish that the full system is globally linear.





\(A\): state-transition or dynamics matrix.
\(B\): input matrix.
\(C\): observation matrix.
\(D\): direct input-to-output matrix.
\(x,u,y\): state, input, and observation.
\(e^{At}\): matrix exponential for the constant-\(A\) homogeneous evolution.
\(T\): invertible state-coordinate transformation.
\(A' = TAT^{-1}\): similar dynamics matrix in transformed coordinates.
\(c,d\): state and observation affine offsets, excluded from a strictly linear rule.

Distinction

For
\[

\qquad a>0,
\]
\[

=

title: Linear Dynamical System
text: A linear dynamical system has state evolution that is linear in the state and declared inputs, optionally paired with a linear observation model.

title: Linear Dynamical System
text: Linear systems are interpretable baselines with tractable propagation and solution structure; exact probabilistic inference requires additional assumptions such as Gaussian noise. title: Linear Dynamical System

title: Latent Variable
text:
A latent variable is a variable included in a model but not directly observed in the available data and related to observations through the model; it may be inferred conditionally or integrated out.



Latent variables can provide compact explanations of dependence, hidden state, unmeasured causes, or structured variability. Their meaning comes from a specified model and evidence, not from being low-dimensional or visually interpretable.



Suppose several measurements covary because the model posits a smaller set of unobserved quantities that influence them. Those unobserved quantities are latent variables. Different models can assign different latent variables to the same observations.



Let \(y\) denote observed data and \(z\) a latent variable. A latent-variable model specifies a joint or conditional structure such as
\[
p(y,z)=p(y\mid z)\,p(z),
\]
while only \(y\) is directly available. Depending on the task, the model may integrate over \(z\) to obtain a marginal distribution \(p(y)\), infer \(p(z\mid y)\), or report a point summary of that conditional distribution.
In the inspected probabilistic PCA model,
\[
y=Wz+\mu+\varepsilon,
\]
where \(z\) is latent, \(W\) links latent and observed variables, and \(\varepsilon\) is an observation-error term (Tipping and Bishop 1999). This is one example, not the definition of every latent variable.




\(y\): observed variable or data vector.
\(z\): latent or unobserved variable.
\(p(z)\): prior or population model for the latent variable.
\(p(y\mid z)\): observation model.
\(p(z\mid y)\): inferred posterior distribution.
\(W\): one possible mapping from latent to observed coordinates.




Assumed background: elementary probability notation. No existing LDG Knowledge Object is required.










Concept
Distinction




State
A state is defined by its role in continuing a system description. A latent variable is defined by being unobserved in a model. A latent variable may represent state, a parameter, a cause, or another hidden quantity.


Observation
Observations are available measurements; latent variables are inferred through a model relating them to observations.


Feature or representation
A computed feature can be directly observed from data after transformation. Calling it latent requires a generative or inferential role, not merely compression.


Low-dimensional coordinate
Latent variables can be high-dimensional, and a low-dimensional embedding can be deterministic rather than latent-variable inference.


Ground-truth cause
A fitted latent variable need not correspond uniquely to a physical or biological cause.






A latent variable does not imply:

that it is a true hidden mechanism or uniquely identifiable quantity;
low dimensionality, smooth geometry, or dynamical state;
that decoding or reconstruction validates its interpretation;
that different fitted coordinate systems represent different mechanisms;
causal influence on observations; or
that residual variation is meaningless noise.




Let \(z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) and
\[
y_1=z+\varepsilon_1,\qquad
y_2=2z+\varepsilon_2.
\]
The observed variables \(y_1,y_2\) are measured; \(z\) is latent. Their correlation can support the model, but finite observations generally do not reveal a unique realized \(z\) or prove that this particular hidden variable generated the data.



Neural population analyses often use latent variables to summarize shared structure across many recorded units (Cunningham and Yu 2014). Such variables can support prediction and hypothesis formation, but a low-dimensional representation is not by itself evidence of a neural mechanism.



Latent Variable begins the bridge from dynamical state concepts to observation and inference. It gives LDG a place to separate model-hidden quantities from measured variables, geometric coordinates, and mechanistic claims.




Which transformations of a latent variable preserve the same scientific interpretation?
When should a latent variable be interpreted as dynamical state rather than a static factor?
What interventions or cross-condition tests can constrain its meaning?





Tipping and Bishop give an inspected primary example of a probabilistic latent-variable model relating unobserved variables to observations (Tipping and Bishop 1999).
Cunningham and Yu review latent variables in neural population dimensionality reduction and caution that population representations must be connected to testable mechanisms (Cunningham and Yu 2014).

title: Kernel
text:
In LDG’s temporal-modeling context, a kernel is a weighting function that specifies how input values at different lags contribute to an output through a linear operator.



Kernels provide a simple alternative to latent state dynamics: output can depend on a weighted history of inputs without positing an evolving hidden state. The word is overloaded, so the temporal convention must be explicit.



Slide a weighting curve over the recent input history. Multiply input values by lag-dependent weights and sum them to produce the current output.



For a causal continuous-time linear time-invariant system with zero initial state, no direct feedthrough, and input taken as zero before initialization,
\[
y(t)=\int_0^\infty k(\tau)u(t-\tau)\,d\tau.
\]
In discrete time,
\[
y_k=\sum_{\ell\ge0}k_\ell u_{k-\ell}.
\]
The function \(k\) is the temporal kernel; under these conventions it is the ordinary function-valued impulse response. A direct-feedthrough term requires separate treatment or a generalized kernel containing an impulse. Åström and Murray derive the state-space convolution representation (Åström and Murray 2021, sec. 6.3).




\(k(\tau)\) or \(k_\ell\): kernel weight at lag.
\(u\): input signal.
\(y\): output signal.
\(\tau\) or \(\ell\): lag.




Assumed background: elementary sums, integrals, and linear weighting. Convolution is the next planned Concept Object and is therefore not used as metadata.










Concept
Distinction




Impulse response
For an LTI system, the temporal kernel equals the impulse response.


State-space model
Represents internal evolving state; a kernel is an input-output operator and may omit an explicit state representation.


Machine-learning kernel
A similarity or positive-definite function used by kernel methods; not the temporal meaning adopted here.


Smoothing window
A chosen kernel used for preprocessing; it need not be a generative system response.






A kernel does not imply causality unless its support is restricted, time invariance unless it depends only on lag, linearity of the underlying biological mechanism, finite memory, or uniqueness from finite noisy data.



For \(k(\tau)=e^{-\tau}\mathbf 1_{\tau\ge0}\), recent input receives more weight than distant input. For zero initial state and input zero before initialization, the same response is represented by \(\dot x=-x+u\), \(y=x\), showing that kernel and state-space descriptions can be alternative representations.



Temporal receptive fields, hemodynamic response functions, and stimulus-response filters are often represented by kernels. A fitted kernel can predict time-locked responses without establishing a latent dynamical mechanism.



Kernel establishes the fixed-filter baseline needed to ask when a latent dynamical-system model is warranted.

How should nonlinear or time-varying response operators be represented?
What regularization preserves interpretable lag structure?





Åström and Murray give the inspected impulse-response and convolution representation of LTI systems (Åström and Murray 2021, sec. 6.3).

The function \(k\) is the temporal kernel; under these conventions it is the ordinary function-valued impulse response. A direct-feedthrough term requires separate treatment or a generalized kernel containing an impulse. Åström and Murray derive the state-space convolution representation (Åström and Murray 2021, sec. 6.3).

title: Kernel
text:
\(k(\tau)\) or \(k_\ell\): kernel weight at lag.
\(u\): input signal.
\(y\): output signal.
\(\tau\) or \(\ell\): lag.

title: Kernel
text: Assumed background: elementary sums, integrals, and linear weighting. Convolution is the next planned Concept Object and is therefore not used as metadata.

title: Kernel
text:
Concept
Distinction




Impulse response
For an LTI system, the temporal kernel equals the impulse response.


State-space model
Represents internal evolving state; a kernel is an input-output operator and may omit an explicit state representation.


Machine-learning kernel
A similarity or positive-definite function used by kernel methods; not the temporal meaning adopted here.


Smoothing window
A chosen kernel used for preprocessing; it need not be a generative system response.

title: Kernel
text: A kernel does not imply causality unless its support is restricted, time invariance unless it depends only on lag, linearity of the underlying biological mechanism, finite memory, or uniqueness from finite noisy data.

title: Kernel
text: For \(k(\tau)=e^{-\tau}\mathbf 1_{\tau\ge0}\), recent input receives more weight than distant input. For zero initial state and input zero before initialization, the same response is represented by \(\dot x=-x+u\), \(y=x\), showing that kernel and state-space descriptions can be alternative representations.

title: Kernel
text: Temporal receptive fields, hemodynamic response functions, and stimulus-response filters are often represented by kernels. A fitted kernel can predict time-locked responses without establishing a latent dynamical mechanism.

title: Kernel
text: Kernel establishes the fixed-filter baseline needed to ask when a latent dynamical-system model is warranted.
