title: Input-Driven Dynamics
text:
Input-driven dynamics describe state evolution whose instantaneous or stepwise update depends on an external input signal in addition to the current state.



Many neural, behavioral, and engineered systems are not closed autonomous systems. Stimuli, commands, sensory feedback, context, and interventions may alter the state evolution. If those influences are omitted, input effects can be misread as state-dependent autonomous dynamics.



An autonomous rule asks, “Given the current state, what happens next?” An input-driven rule asks, “Given the current state and the externally supplied input now or over an interval, what happens next?”



For the smooth-manifold formulation, let \(\mathcal X\) be a smooth \(n\)-manifold, \(\mathcal U\) an input-value space, and \(\Theta\) a parameter space. A continuous-time input-driven model can be written
\[
\dot x(t)=f\bigl(t,x(t),u(t);\theta\bigr),
\qquad
f(t,x,u;\theta)\in T_x\mathcal X,
\]
In the Euclidean special case, \(\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(f:\mathbb R\times\mathcal X\times\mathcal U\times\Theta\to\mathbb R^n\). A discrete-time model has the form
\[
x_{k+1}=F_k(x_k,u_k;\theta).
\]
Here \(F_k:\mathcal X\times\mathcal U\times\Theta\to\mathcal X\).
Here \(x\) is the state, \(u\) is an externally supplied argument under the declared system boundary, and \(\theta\) denotes parameters held fixed for the modeled evolution. Åström and Murray use the corresponding separation among state, control/input, and measured output (Åström and Murray 2021, sec. 3.2).
A particular initial condition and input history determine a trajectory only after declaring an admissible input class—such as measurable or piecewise-continuous \(\mathcal U\)-valued functions—and imposing causal dependence, existence, uniqueness, admissibility, and regularity assumptions. Causal dependence means that two admissible inputs agreeing on \([t_0,t]\) produce the same state at \(t\) when the initial condition and parameters agree. Without uniqueness, \(\Phi\) may be a set-valued relation rather than a single transition operator. Those theorem-level conditions are not supplied by the notation alone.


Write the state reached at time \(t\) from \((t_0,x_0)\) under an input segment as
\[
x(t)
=
\Phi(t,t_0,x_0;u_{[t_0,t]}).
\]
For \(t_0\le s\le t\), consistent input-conditioned evolution satisfies the segment-concatenation law
\[
\Phi(t,t_0,x_0;u_{[t_0,t]})
=
\Phi\left(
t,s,
\Phi(s,t_0,x_0;u_{[t_0,s]});
u_{[s,t]}
\right),
\]
whenever all terms are defined and the two restrictions are compatible pieces of the same input history. The zero-duration identity is \(\Phi(t_0,t_0,x;\varnothing)=x\). This two-parameter segment law is not called a cocycle here; cocycle notation requires a defined input-shift/base dynamics. This is not the autonomous one-parameter flow law: the later transition depends on the later input segment, and changing the input can change the trajectory even when the initial state is fixed.
Two bounded special cases can define new autonomous models when the original rule has no explicit clock dependence. A fixed input \(u(t)\equiv\bar u\) gives \(f_{\bar u}(x)=f(x,\bar u;\theta)\). A state-feedback rule \(u=\kappa(x)\) gives the closed-loop vector field \(f_{\mathrm{cl}}(x)=f(x,\kappa(x);\theta)\). These are newly declared rules; neither turns the full family of arbitrary input histories into one shared autonomous flow.
For discrete time, define a multi-step transition by
\[
x_k
=
\Phi_{k:j}(x_j;u_j,\ldots,u_{k-1}),
\qquad k>j.
\]
Splitting at \(m\) gives
\[
\Phi_{k:j}(x_j;u_j,\ldots,u_{k-1})
=
\Phi_{k:m}\left(
\Phi_{m:j}(x_j;u_j,\ldots,u_{m-1});
u_m,\ldots,u_{k-1}
\right).
\]
The discrete identity transition is \(\Phi_{j:j}=\operatorname{id}\).




An input is an external argument to the transition rule under the chosen boundary; it may be time-varying or constant.
A control is an input selected according to a declared decision rule or agent. Not every input is controlled.
An intervention is an experimental or causal manipulation. Representing it as an input does not by itself identify its causal effect.
A parameter specifies the rule and is held fixed within the declared evolution, unless a new model promotes it to state or input.
Process noise is a stochastic transition disturbance under a probability model; an observed input is not process noise, and an unknown input is not automatically random.
An observation is generated from the state through an observation model. Feedback can make an observation inform a future control, but the observation and control retain different roles.




Suppose the original rule is time-independent, \(\dot x=f(x,u;\theta)\), and an input is generated by another modeled system,
\[
\dot z=g(z),
\qquad
u=\rho(z).
\]
Then the augmented state \((x,z)\) may obey an autonomous rule
\[
\frac{d}{dt}
\begin{pmatrix}x\\z\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}f(x,\rho(z);\theta)\\g(z)\end{pmatrix}.
\]
This is a new system boundary and a new state space. It requires a specified input-generator model, its initial state, and the relevant well-posedness assumptions. If the original rule depends explicitly on clock time, the clock must also be modeled—for example by adding \(\dot\tau=1\)—or the augmented system remains nonautonomous. An arbitrary prescribed or unknown input history may require infinite-dimensional memory and cannot be made finite-dimensional and autonomous merely by relabeling it as state.





\(x(t)\): the system state.
\(u(t)\): external input under the declared system boundary.
\(f(t,x,u;\theta)\): continuous-time state-change rule.
\(F_k(x,u;\theta)\): discrete-time update rule.
\(\theta\): parameters held fixed in the declared evolution.
\(u_{[t_0,t]}\): the input history relevant to evolution over an interval.
\(\Phi(t,t_0,x_0;u_{[t_0,t]})\): input-conditioned transition operator.
\(\Phi_{k:j}\): discrete multi-step transition driven by an input sequence.
\(z\): state of a modeled input generator in an augmented system.




Vector Field provides the local state-change idea. Flow provides the autonomous finite-time comparison that input-conditioned evolution must not be silently conflated with.










Concept
Distinction




Autonomous dynamics
Depend only on the current state under fixed parameters; input-driven dynamics depend explicitly on an external signal.


Parameter
The distinction is a declared modeling role, not whether a realized value changes. A parameter specifies the evolution rule under the model, whereas an input is an externally supplied argument to that rule; a constant signal can still be an input.


Process noise
A stochastic transition disturbance under a declared probability model. A measured input, unknown deterministic input, and process noise are not interchangeable.


Control
An input chosen by a controller or policy. The model role does not by itself establish experimental control or causal effect.


Intervention
A manipulation of a system or environment. Encoding it as \(u\) does not by itself establish identifiability or causal interpretation.


Observation
An observation reports on state; an input influences its evolution. The same physical quantity can change roles under a different system boundary.


Augmented state
An input-generating process can be incorporated only by specifying its own dynamics and initial state, thereby changing the system boundary.


Autonomous flow
Depends on state and elapsed time under one autonomous rule. Input-conditioned transitions also depend on compatible input segments and obey a concatenation law rather than a bare one-parameter flow law.






Input-driven dynamics do not imply:

that the input is known, measured without error, or experimentally controlled;
that state and input effects are identifiable from passive data;
linearity, time invariance, or additivity of input effects;
that an autonomous flow exists on the original state space;
that unexplained variation should be labeled input; or
that including an input proves a causal influence;
that the input is identifiable separately from state, parameters, or noise;
controllability, observability, or robustness;
that segment composition is an autonomous group or semigroup law; or
that arbitrary unknown inputs can be absorbed into a finite-dimensional state.




For a leaky integrator,
\[
\dot x(t)=-a x(t)+b u(t),\qquad a>0,
\]
the same initial state can produce different trajectories under different input functions. If \(u(t)\equiv0\), the special case is autonomous; changing \(u\) changes the evolution without changing the initial state. More explicitly,
\[
x(t)=e^{-a(t-t_0)}x_0+b\int_{t_0}^{t}e^{-a(t-s)}u(s)\,ds.
\]
The integral exhibits dependence on the full input segment. Splitting it at an intermediate time reproduces the transition-composition law.



Sensory stimuli, task cues, motor commands, rewards, and perturbations are candidate inputs under suitable system boundaries. Their inclusion can separate externally driven changes from recurrent state evolution, but observational correlations alone do not identify the direction of influence.



At L2, Input-Driven Dynamics provides typed continuous/discrete rules, input-history-dependent transition operators, and their segment-concatenation law. It prevents LDG from forcing all trajectories into an autonomous shared-flow interpretation and prepares comparisons among controlled, driven, noisy, kernel-based, and latent dynamical models.

When can an unknown input be inferred separately from latent state?
What baseline should an input-driven latent model beat?





Åström and Murray provide the inspected input–state–output state-space formulation and linear input example (Åström and Murray 2021, sec. 3.2). Section numbering was checked against the inspected 24 July 2020 electronic second-edition manuscript corresponding to the published edition.
Unknown-input inference, controllability, observability, causal identification, and robustness theorems are intentionally deferred.





Defines continuous- and discrete-time input dependence.
Makes input history explicit in finite-time evolution.
Separates inputs, parameters, noise, observations, and augmented states.
Avoids treating input-conditioned evolution as an autonomous flow.
Types continuous and discrete input-driven state equations and fixed parameters.
Defines input-history transitions and compatible segment concatenation.
Separates inputs, controls, interventions, parameters, process noise, and observations.
States the model and boundary requirements for autonomous state augmentation.
Defers unknown-input inference, controllability, causality, and robustness theory.

title: Concepts
text: Concept Objects define terminology, intuition, formal meaning, adjacent concepts, non-implications, and relevance to LDG. The sections below provide a public reading order through the current concept library.

title: Concepts
text:
Foundational dynamics

State — what information counts as the state of a specified system at a time. (L1, stable)
State Space — the admissible state values under a specified state description. (L1, stable)
Trajectory — one admissible system evolution parameterized by system time. (L1, stable)
Phase Space — a state space read as the arena of dynamical trajectories. (L2, stable)
Initial Condition — a state value assigned at a reference time. (L1, stable)
Vector Field — a local instantaneous state-change rule. (L2, stable)
Flow — finite-time evolution across supported initial states. (L2, stable)
Fixed Point — a state unchanged by the specified evolution. (L2, stable)
Stability — response of a declared dynamical object to specified perturbations. (L2, stable)
Attractor — an invariant set approached from a surrounding basin. (L2, stable)
Limit Cycle — an isolated periodic orbit with separately stated stability. (L2, stable)
Input-Driven Dynamics — evolution depending on state and an external input signal. (L2, stable)

title: Concepts
text:
Latent-variable foundations

Latent Variable — a model variable not directly observed in the available data. (L1, stable)
Observation Model — the relation from latent or system variables to measurements. (L2, stable)
State-Space Model — a joint transition and observation description. (L2, stable)
Linear Dynamical System — linear state evolution with optional inputs and outputs. (L2, stable)
Process Noise — stochastic disturbance entering state evolution. (L2, stable)
Observation Noise — stochastic measurement variability conditional on state. (L2, stable)
Identifiability — uniqueness of model specifications from observable distributions. (L2, stable)

title: Concepts
text:
Temporal / kernel foundations

Kernel — lag-dependent weighting in a temporal linear operator. (L1, stable)
Convolution — lag-weighted combination of a signal and kernel. (L2, stable)
Deconvolution — noise-sensitive inversion of a convolutional observation model. (L2, stable)

title: Concepts
text:
Geometry foundations

Ambient Dimension — dimension of the surrounding representation space. (L1, stable)
Intrinsic Dimension — degrees of freedom under a declared model, scale, and criterion. (L1, stable)
Linear Subspace — a subset closed under linear combinations. (L1, stable)
Embedding — an injective structure-preserving representation into another space. (L1, stable)
Manifold — a locally Euclidean space with compatible smooth charts. (L1, stable)
Tangent Space — the local vector space of first-order directions at a point. (L2, stable)
Metric — a point-to-point distance satisfying the metric axioms. (L2, stable)
Geodesic — a locally straight zero-acceleration curve under chosen geometry. (L2, stable)
Riemannian Metric — a smooth field of tangent-space inner products. (L2, stable)
Curvature — departure from flat geometry under a declared curvature notion. (L2, stable)
Topology — neighborhood and continuity structure defined by open sets. (L1, stable)
Circle / S¹ — one periodic coordinate with circular topology. (L1, stable)
Torus — the product of two circles or two periodic coordinates. (L1, stable)
Latent Trajectory — a time-indexed latent random path, its posterior law, or a declared realization/summary. (L2, stable)
Dynamics on Manifolds — tangent vector fields and flows constrained to a manifold. (L2, stable)

title: Geodesic
text:
An affinely parameterized geodesic is a curve that follows the locally straight, zero-covariant-acceleration paths determined by a chosen connection, and for a Riemannian metric is locally length-minimizing over sufficiently short segments.



Geodesics generalize straight lines to curved spaces. They are often called shortest paths, but a geodesic need not minimize distance globally or beyond special local intervals.



Great circles are geodesics on a sphere. A short arc is the shortest route between nearby points, while a sufficiently long arc may not be globally shortest.



Let \(M\) be a smooth manifold with a linear connection \(\nabla\), and let \(\gamma:I\to M\) be smooth. Its covariant acceleration is
\[
D_t\dot\gamma
=
\nabla_{\dot\gamma}\dot\gamma.
\]
An affinely parameterized geodesic satisfies
\[
D_t\dot\gamma=0.
\]
In local coordinates \(x^1,\ldots,x^n\), this is the system
\[
\ddot x^k(t)
+
\Gamma^k_{ij}(x(t))\dot x^i(t)\dot x^j(t)
=0,
\]
where \(\Gamma^k_{ij}\) are the Christoffel symbols of the chosen connection in that chart (Lee 1997, ch. 4). They are coordinate coefficients, not tensor components by themselves; connection construction and transformation proofs are deferred.


For \(p\in M\), \(v\in T_pM\), and initial time \(t_0\), the geodesic initial-value problem is
\[
\gamma(t_0)=p,
\qquad
\dot\gamma(t_0)=v.
\]
Under the smooth-connection assumptions, these data determine a unique local geodesic and a unique maximal extension on an open interval containing \(t_0\) (Lee 1997, ch. 4). Maximal does not mean defined for all real time; that stronger property is geodesic completeness.



If \(\gamma(t)\) is a geodesic and \(a\ne0\), then \(\widetilde\gamma(s)=\gamma(as+b)\) is again an affinely parameterized geodesic. A general nonlinear reparameterization usually adds acceleration parallel to the curve and does not satisfy the zero-acceleration equation, even though it traces the same path image. Unparameterized geodesic paths and affine geodesics must therefore be distinguished.



For a Riemannian Metric, the relevant connection is the unique torsion-free, metric-compatible Levi–Civita connection. Its geodesics have constant speed because their velocity is parallel along the curve (Lee 1997, ch. 5). Every Riemannian geodesic is locally minimizing on sufficiently short intervals, and every length-minimizing smooth curve is a geodesic when given an affine (in particular, constant-speed) parametrization. These are local statements: a geodesic can cease to minimize after leaving a normal neighborhood, and multiple geodesics can join the same endpoints (Lee 1997, ch. 6).



Let \(\gamma_v\) denote the maximal geodesic with \(\gamma_v(0)=p\) and \(\dot\gamma_v(0)=v\). The exponential map is
\[
\exp_p(v)=\gamma_v(1)
\]
for tangent vectors \(v\) whose geodesic is defined at time \(1\). Equivalently, \(\exp_p(tv)=\gamma_v(t)\) where defined. Near the zero vector, \(\exp_p\) provides normal coordinates and a local relation between tangent vectors and nearby points. It is not generally globally injective or defined on all of \(T_pM\) without completeness assumptions.





\(\gamma:I\to M\): curve.
\(\dot\gamma\): velocity.
\(\nabla_{\dot\gamma}\dot\gamma\): covariant acceleration.
\(L(\gamma)\): Riemannian curve length.
\(\Gamma^k_{ij}\): Christoffel symbols of the chosen connection.
\(p,v\): initial point and tangent velocity.
\(\gamma_v\): maximal geodesic determined by \(v\in T_pM\).
\(\exp_p\): exponential map on its supported tangent-domain.

title: Geodesic
text: An affinely parameterized geodesic is a curve that follows the locally straight, zero-covariant-acceleration paths determined by a chosen connection, and for a Riemannian metric is locally length-minimizing over sufficiently short segments.

title: Geodesic
text: Geodesics generalize straight lines to curved spaces. They are often called shortest paths, but a geodesic need not minimize distance globally or beyond special local intervals.

title: Geodesic
text: Great circles are geodesics on a sphere. A short arc is the shortest route between nearby points, while a sufficiently long arc may not be globally shortest.

title: Geodesic
text:
Let \(M\) be a smooth manifold with a linear connection \(\nabla\), and let \(\gamma:I\to M\) be smooth. Its covariant acceleration is
\[
D_t\dot\gamma
=
\nabla_{\dot\gamma}\dot\gamma.
\]
An affinely parameterized geodesic satisfies
\[
D_t\dot\gamma=0.
\]
In local coordinates \(x^1,\ldots,x^n\), this is the system
\[
\ddot x^k(t)
+
\Gamma^k_{ij}(x(t))\dot x^i(t)\dot x^j(t)
=0,
\]
where \(\Gamma^k_{ij}\) are the Christoffel symbols of the chosen connection in that chart (Lee 1997, ch. 4). They are coordinate coefficients, not tensor components by themselves; connection construction and transformation proofs are deferred.


For \(p\in M\), \(v\in T_pM\), and initial time \(t_0\), the geodesic initial-value problem is
\[
\gamma(t_0)=p,
\qquad
\dot\gamma(t_0)=v.
\]
Under the smooth-connection assumptions, these data determine a unique local geodesic and a unique maximal extension on an open interval containing \(t_0\) (Lee 1997, ch. 4). Maximal does not mean defined for all real time; that stronger property is geodesic completeness.



If \(\gamma(t)\) is a geodesic and \(a\ne0\), then \(\widetilde\gamma(s)=\gamma(as+b)\) is again an affinely parameterized geodesic. A general nonlinear reparameterization usually adds acceleration parallel to the curve and does not satisfy the zero-acceleration equation, even though it traces the same path image. Unparameterized geodesic paths and affine geodesics must therefore be distinguished.



For a Riemannian Metric, the relevant connection is the unique torsion-free, metric-compatible Levi–Civita connection. Its geodesics have constant speed because their velocity is parallel along the curve (Lee 1997, ch. 5). Every Riemannian geodesic is locally minimizing on sufficiently short intervals, and every length-minimizing smooth curve is a geodesic when given an affine (in particular, constant-speed) parametrization. These are local statements: a geodesic can cease to minimize after leaving a normal neighborhood, and multiple geodesics can join the same endpoints (Lee 1997, ch. 6).



Let \(\gamma_v\) denote the maximal geodesic with \(\gamma_v(0)=p\) and \(\dot\gamma_v(0)=v\). The exponential map is
\[
\exp_p(v)=\gamma_v(1)
\]
for tangent vectors \(v\) whose geodesic is defined at time \(1\). Equivalently, \(\exp_p(tv)=\gamma_v(t)\) where defined. Near the zero vector, \(\exp_p\) provides normal coordinates and a local relation between tangent vectors and nearby points. It is not generally globally injective or defined on all of \(T_pM\) without completeness assumptions.

title: Fixed Point
text:
A fixed point is a state that remains unchanged under the specified evolution for every supported elapsed time.



Fixed points describe stationary behaviors of a dynamical model. They provide reference states around which local stability, linearization, basins, and transitions can later be studied. Existence and stability are separate questions: a state can be fixed yet unstable.



Place the system exactly at a fixed point and let its rule act. The state does not move. This says nothing yet about what happens when the initial state is slightly displaced.



For a local flow with supported domain \(W\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathcal X\), \(x^\ast\in\mathcal X\) is a fixed point when
\[
\phi_\tau(x^\ast)=x^\ast
\]
for every supported elapsed time \((\tau,x^\ast)\in W\). Equivalently, its orbit is the singleton \(\{x^\ast\}\) and its associated trajectory is constant. Teschl uses fixed, stationary, and equilibrium point for this constant-orbit case (Teschl 2012, sec. 6.3).
For an autonomous differential equation
\[
\dot x=f(x),
\]
a candidate equilibrium satisfies
\[
f(x^\ast)=0.
\]
This zero guarantees that \(x(t)\equiv x^\ast\) is a constant solution. Under the regularity and uniqueness assumptions that generate the single-valued local flow described in the stable Math Object, it is equivalent to \(\phi_\tau(x^\ast)=x^\ast\) on the supported domain. The converse from flow-fixedness to \(f(x^\ast)=0\) also uses the elapsed-time generator/differentiability relation. Without uniqueness, the constant solution can coexist with other solutions through the same initial state, so a bare zero of \(f\) does not by itself supply a unique flow (Teschl 2012, secs. 1.3, 2.2, 6.2–6.3).
The identity \(\phi_0(x)=x\) holds for every state and therefore does not establish fixedness. Likewise, \(\phi_T(p)=p\) for one \(T>0\) may indicate a nontrivial periodic orbit; a continuous-time fixed point remains unchanged for every supported elapsed time and has a singleton orbit.


For a discrete update map \(F:\mathcal X\to\mathcal X\), a point \(p\) is fixed when
\[
F(p)=p.
\]
Its iterates remain constant: \(F^n(p)=p\) for all \(n\ge0\). A periodic point has prime period \(k\) when \(k\) is the least positive integer satisfying \(F^k(p)=p\); if \(F^n(p)=p\), the prime period divides \(n\). It is a fixed point of \(F\) only when its prime period is one. Teschl makes this distinction for discrete dynamical systems (Teschl 2012, sec. 10.2). A discrete fixed point is not automatically the fixed point of a continuous-time flow, nor does every update map arise as a time-one flow map.



Fixedness is a property of the represented evolution, not of one coordinate label. For a bijective change of state representation \(h:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y\), define the conjugate discrete map
\[
G=h\circ F\circ h^{-1}.
\]
If \(F(p)=p\), then \(G(h(p))=h(p)\). For a conjugated flow,
\[
\psi_\tau=h\circ\phi_\tau\circ h^{-1},
\]
fixed points are likewise carried from \(p\) to \(h(p)\), with supported domains transported by \(h\). For vector-field coordinates, a time-independent \(C^1\) diffeomorphism gives
\[
g(y)=Dh\bigl(h^{-1}(y)\bigr)f\bigl(h^{-1}(y)\bigr),
\]
so \(f(p)=0\) if and only if \(g(h(p))=0\). A non-injective projection or observation map can merge fixed and non-fixed states and does not preserve this conclusion (Teschl 2012, secs. 6.2, 9.3).



For a parameterized family \(f(x;\mu)\), equilibria solve \(f(x^\ast;\mu)=0\) at a specified parameter value. Whether an equilibrium continues, disappears, splits, or changes stability as \(\mu\) changes is a separate persistence or bifurcation question. This Concept records that boundary but defers implicit-function, bifurcation, and stability theorems.





\(x^\ast\): a candidate fixed point.
\(f(x^\ast)=0\): zero instantaneous change for an autonomous vector field.
\(\phi_\tau(x^\ast)=x^\ast\): invariance under finite-time evolution.
\(x(t)\equiv x^\ast\): the constant trajectory through the fixed point.
\(F:\mathcal X\to\mathcal X\): discrete-time update map.
\(\operatorname{Fix}(F)=\{p\in\mathcal X:F(p)=p\}\): set of discrete fixed points.
\(G=h\circ F\circ h^{-1}\): coordinate-conjugate update map.
\(\mu\): parameter held fixed when solving an equilibrium equation.




Vector Field supplies the local condition \(f(x^\ast)=0\). Flow supplies the finite-time invariance statement.
The First-Order Autonomous Dynamical System records the regularity, existence, uniqueness, and local-flow assumptions required for the strongest equivalence statements.










Concept
Distinction from fixed point




Initial condition
Any admissible state can be an initial condition; only special states are fixed.


Constant observation
A measurement may appear constant while hidden state variables change.


Stability
Stability concerns the response to nearby perturbations. Fixed-point existence alone does not answer it.


Attractor
Fixedness alone establishes neither attraction nor Lyapunov stability. A point may satisfy an adopted attraction convention only after convergence from a basin is shown, while stability must be assessed separately.


Periodic orbit
A nontrivial periodic orbit returns after a positive period while moving between returns; a fixed point has a constant orbit.


Discrete periodic point
Satisfies \(F^n(p)=p\) for some \(n\); it is fixed only when the prime period is one.


Zero of an estimated vector field
A numerical or fitted root whose scientific status depends on model adequacy, optimization error, and uncertainty.


Equilibrium branch
A parameter-indexed family of fixed points. Its persistence is additional structure, not part of one fixed-point definition.


Fixed point of an operator in an existence theorem
An equation such as \(T(u)=u\) used by the Banach contraction method. It may help prove a differential equation has a solution, but it is not automatically a stationary state of a dynamical evolution (Teschl 2012, sec. 2.1).






A fixed point does not imply:

stability, attraction, robustness, or biological desirability;
uniqueness of the fixed point;
that nearby trajectories are slow;
that a constant recording reveals a fixed latent state;
that the fixed point persists after parameters or inputs change;
that an estimated zero of a fitted vector field is a true system equilibrium;
that a small residual \(\|f(\widehat x)\|\) proves an exact root or an admissible state; or
that a non-injective observation preserves the number or identity of fixed states.




For
\[
\dot x=x(1-x),
\]
\(x^\ast=0\) and \(x^\ast=1\) are fixed points because the right-hand side vanishes at both values. Their shared status as fixed points does not make their nearby behavior identical.
For a discrete example, \(F(x)=-x\) has the fixed point \(0\). Every \(x\ne0\) satisfies \(F^2(x)=x\) but not \(F(x)=x\), so it has prime period two rather than being fixed.



Fixed-point models are often used as hypotheses for persistent activity or settled behavioral states. Such an interpretation requires evidence that the relevant state is stationary under the model and that observed constancy is not produced by measurement saturation, unobserved motion, or a slowly varying trajectory.



At L2, Fixed Point establishes compatible continuous-flow, vector-field, and discrete-map formulations and makes their assumptions explicit. It provides the stationary reference needed for stability and point-attractor analysis without using “equilibrium,” “stable state,” and “attractor” as synonyms.

When do inputs turn an autonomous fixed point into a moving or input-dependent equilibrium?
What observations can distinguish a true fixed state from slow dynamics?

Teschl defines fixed and periodic points of discrete maps and their iterates (Teschl 2012, sec. 10.2).
Teschl supplies the inspected topological-conjugacy and operator-fixed-point contexts used to delimit coordinate invariance and terminology (Teschl 2012, secs. 2.1, 9.3).
The stable Math Object contains the inspected existence, uniqueness, maximal-solution, and local-flow assumptions supporting the continuous-time equivalence.

title: Dynamics on Manifolds
text:
Dynamics on a manifold evolve states within a manifold using a rule whose instantaneous vectors lie in the appropriate tangent spaces.



Many systems have constrained or non-Euclidean state spaces. Manifold dynamics make those constraints part of the state description rather than relying on ambient coordinates that may leave the admissible space.



For motion constrained to a sphere, the instantaneous velocity must be tangent to the sphere. A vector pointing radially outward would leave the state space.



Let \(M\) be a smooth manifold. An autonomous vector field is a smooth section
\[
X:M\to TM,
\qquad
X(p)\in T_pM.
\]
An integral curve is a smooth map \(\gamma:I\to M\) satisfying intrinsically
\[
\dot\gamma(t)=X(\gamma(t)).
\]
In a chart \(x=(x^1,\ldots,x^n)\) with
\[
X=X^i(x)\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i},
\]
the integral-curve equation becomes
\[
\dot x^i(t)=X^i(x(t)).
\]
A smooth vector field therefore supplies ordinary differential equations in each chart, with compatible expressions on overlaps.


Under the standard local existence and uniqueness assumptions, integral curves define a smooth local flow
\[
\Phi:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R\times M\to M,
\]
where \(\mathcal D\) is an open supported domain containing \(\{0\}\times M\). It satisfies
\[
\Phi(0,p)=p,
\]
and
\[
\Phi(t+s,p)=\Phi(t,\Phi(s,p))
\]
whenever both sides are supported. Completeness is the additional condition \(\mathcal D=\mathbb R\times M\); tangency and smoothness alone do not imply it (Mrowka 2004, sec. 20.1; Teschl 2012, ch. 6).



If \(y=h(x)\) is a smooth coordinate change, the vector-field components transform by
\[
Y^a(y)
=
\frac{\partial h^a}{\partial x^i}(x)X^i(x),
\qquad x=h^{-1}(y).
\]
Thus coordinate formulas can look different while representing the same intrinsic vector field and integral curves. A non-invertible projection or learned representation does not automatically preserve the vector field.



Suppose an embedded state manifold is a regular level set
\[
M=\{q\in\mathbb R^D:c(q)=0\},
\]
where \(c:\mathbb R^D\to\mathbb R^r\) is smooth and \(Dc_q\) has full rank on \(M\). Then
\[
T_qM=\ker Dc_q.
\]
An ambient vector field \(F:\mathbb R^D\to\mathbb R^D\) is tangent along \(M\) when
\[
Dc_qF(q)=0,
\qquad q\in M.
\]
Under local uniqueness, restricting such a smooth tangent field to \(M\) produces manifold-valued integral curves. The algebraic constraint and tangency condition do not by themselves establish global existence, boundary viability, numerical preservation, or adequacy of \(M\) as the real state space.



An ambient numerical update such as
\[
q_{n+1}=\Pi_M(q_n+hF(q_n))
\]
or a retraction update
\[
q_{n+1}=R_{q_n}(hX(q_n))
\]
can keep iterates on or near \(M\). These are discretization schemes, not the exact flow \(\Phi_h\). Projection/retraction choice can alter the dynamics; consistency, order, constraint error, invariant preservation, and convergence must be evaluated. A plotted constraint-preserving trajectory does not prove that the numerical map approximates the intended intrinsic vector field.



A manifold and tangent vector field define dynamics without a metric. A Riemannian metric can define gradient dynamics \(X=-\operatorname{grad}_gV\) or other metric-dependent rules. Geodesic motion is a special second-order/connection-governed evolution, not a generic first-order vector field. title: Dynamics on Manifolds
text:
Let \(M\) be a smooth manifold. An autonomous vector field is a smooth section
\[
X:M\to TM,
\qquad
X(p)\in T_pM.
\]
An integral curve is a smooth map \(\gamma:I\to M\) satisfying intrinsically
\[
\dot\gamma(t)=X(\gamma(t)).
\]
In a chart \(x=(x^1,\ldots,x^n)\) with
\[
X=X^i(x)\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i},
\]
the integral-curve equation becomes
\[
\dot x^i(t)=X^i(x(t)).
\]
A smooth vector field therefore supplies ordinary differential equations in each chart, with compatible expressions on overlaps.


Under the standard local existence and uniqueness assumptions, integral curves define a smooth local flow
\[
\Phi:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R\times M\to M,
\]
where \(\mathcal D\) is an open supported domain containing \(\{0\}\times M\). It satisfies
\[
\Phi(0,p)=p,
\]
and
\[
\Phi(t+s,p)=\Phi(t,\Phi(s,p))
\]
whenever both sides are supported. Completeness is the additional condition \(\mathcal D=\mathbb R\times M\); tangency and smoothness alone do not imply it (Mrowka 2004, sec. 20.1; Teschl 2012, ch. 6).



If \(y=h(x)\) is a smooth coordinate change, the vector-field components transform by
\[
Y^a(y)
=
\frac{\partial h^a}{\partial x^i}(x)X^i(x),
\qquad x=h^{-1}(y).
\]
Thus coordinate formulas can look different while representing the same intrinsic vector field and integral curves. A non-invertible projection or learned representation does not automatically preserve the vector field.



Suppose an embedded state manifold is a regular level set
\[
M=\{q\in\mathbb R^D:c(q)=0\},
\]
where \(c:\mathbb R^D\to\mathbb R^r\) is smooth and \(Dc_q\) has full rank on \(M\). Then
\[
T_qM=\ker Dc_q.
\]
An ambient vector field \(F:\mathbb R^D\to\mathbb R^D\) is tangent along \(M\) when
\[
Dc_qF(q)=0,
\qquad q\in M.
\]
Under local uniqueness, restricting such a smooth tangent field to \(M\) produces manifold-valued integral curves. The algebraic constraint and tangency condition do not by themselves establish global existence, boundary viability, numerical preservation, or adequacy of \(M\) as the real state space.



An ambient numerical update such as
\[
q_{n+1}=\Pi_M(q_n+hF(q_n))
\]
or a retraction update
\[
q_{n+1}=R_{q_n}(hX(q_n))
\]
can keep iterates on or near \(M\). These are discretization schemes, not the exact flow \(\Phi_h\). Projection/retraction choice can alter the dynamics; consistency, order, constraint error, invariant preservation, and convergence must be evaluated. A plotted constraint-preserving trajectory does not prove that the numerical map approximates the intended intrinsic vector field.

title: Curvature
text:
Curvature quantifies how a chosen geometric structure departs from flat geometry, with the precise meaning depending on the curvature object and sign convention in use.



Curvature can describe how tangent directions change, how geodesics converge or diverge, and how local geometry differs from Euclidean space. It is not one universal scalar and should not be inferred from visible bending alone.



On a sphere, initially parallel geodesics can converge; in negatively curved geometry they tend to spread. Intrinsic curvature can be measured within the surface without reference to how it bends in an ambient space.



Let \((M,g)\) be a Riemannian manifold with Levi–Civita connection \(\nabla\). LDG adopts Lee’s convention
\[
R(X,Y)Z
=
\nabla_X\nabla_YZ
-
\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ
-
\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z.
\]
This is the Riemann curvature endomorphism, equivalently a \((1,3)\) tensor. The covariant curvature tensor is
\[
\operatorname{Rm}(X,Y,Z,W)
=
g(R(X,Y)Z,W).
\]
Some authors reverse the sign of \(R\) or permute arguments in \(\operatorname{Rm}\); formulas and signs must therefore be compared only after conventions are aligned (Lee 1997, ch. 7).
Under this convention the covariant tensor satisfies
\[
\operatorname{Rm}(X,Y,Z,W)
=-\operatorname{Rm}(Y,X,Z,W),
\]
\[
\operatorname{Rm}(X,Y,Z,W)
=-\operatorname{Rm}(X,Y,W,Z),
\]
\[
\operatorname{Rm}(X,Y,Z,W)
=\operatorname{Rm}(Z,W,X,Y),
\]
along with the algebraic Bianchi identity. Proofs are deferred.


For a two-dimensional plane \(\Pi\subset T_pM\) with basis \(X,Y\), its sectional curvature is
\[
K(\Pi)=K(X,Y)
=
\frac{\operatorname{Rm}(X,Y,Y,X)}
{g(X,X)g(Y,Y)-g(X,Y)^2}.
\]
The denominator is the squared area of the parallelogram spanned by \(X,Y\), so the value is independent of the chosen basis of \(\Pi\). If \(X,Y\) are orthonormal, \(K(\Pi)=\operatorname{Rm}(X,Y,Y,X)\) (Lee 1997, ch. 8).



For an orthonormal basis \(E_1,\ldots,E_n\) of \(T_pM\), the Ricci tensor is the contraction
\[
\operatorname{Ric}(X,Y)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\operatorname{Rm}(E_i,X,Y,E_i),
\]
consistent with Lee’s sign/order convention. Scalar curvature is the metric trace
\[
S
=
\operatorname{tr}_g\operatorname{Ric}
=
\sum_{j=1}^{n}\operatorname{Ric}(E_j,E_j).
\]
For a unit vector \(V\), \(\operatorname{Ric}(V,V)\) sums sectional curvatures of orthonormal planes containing \(V\), while scalar curvature sums the corresponding ordered sectional contributions. These contractions summarize rather than replace the full curvature tensor.



In coordinates, \(R\) and \(\operatorname{Rm}\) have component arrays such as \(R^\ell{}_{ijk}\) and \(R_{ijkl}\). The arrays transform tensorially even though formulas used to compute them contain non-tensorial Christoffel symbols. Vanishing/nonvanishing, sectional curvature, Ricci curvature, and scalar curvature are invariant geometric statements, not properties of one coordinate display.
If \(F:(M,g)\to(N,h)\) is a local isometry, curvature is preserved:
\[
F^*\operatorname{Rm}^{N}=\operatorname{Rm}^{M},
\]
with the corresponding pushforward relation for \(R\). Lee proves curvature is a local-isometry invariant (Lee 1997, ch. 7).



Under the adopted convention:

Euclidean space has \(K=0\);
the round sphere of radius \(r\) has constant sectional curvature \(K=1/r^2\);
hyperbolic space of radius \(r\) has constant sectional curvature \(K=-1/r^2\).

Changing the curvature-tensor sign convention requires changing the component formula so the geometric meanings of positive and negative sectional curvature remain aligned (Lee 1997, ch. 8).





\(R(X,Y)Z\): Riemann curvature endomorphism, equivalently the associated \((1,3)\) tensor.
\(\operatorname{Rm}(X,Y,Z,W)\): covariant Riemann curvature tensor after lowering an index with \(g\).
\(K(\Pi)\): sectional curvature of a two-dimensional tangent plane.
\(\operatorname{Ric}\): Ricci curvature tensor.
\(S=\operatorname{tr}_g\operatorname{Ric}\): scalar curvature.
\(R^\ell{}_{ijk},R_{ijkl}\): coordinate components under the declared convention.




Riemannian Metric supplies lengths, angles, and the canonical connection needed for Riemannian curvature.
Assumed background: vector-field brackets, covariant derivatives, and the Levi–Civita connection. These are used only to state the bounded definition; their derivation is deferred beyond this object.










Concept
Distinction




Extrinsic bending
Depends on an embedding and second fundamental form; intrinsic Riemannian curvature is determined by \(g\) without choosing an ambient embedding. A cylinder is extrinsically bent but intrinsically flat.


Gaussian curvature
On a Riemannian surface it equals the single sectional curvature at each point; in higher dimensions there are many tangent 2-planes.


Principal / mean curvature
Extrinsic hypersurface quantities, not Ricci or scalar curvature.


Nonlinearity
A model can be nonlinear on a flat space, and a curved space can support simple local equations.


Geodesic deviation
One manifestation of curvature, not the definition of every curvature notion.


Topology
Related through global theorems but not synonymous; local curvature does not uniquely determine topology.






Curvature does not imply visible bending, nonlinear dynamics, a unique scalar summary, a specific topology, better prediction, or reliable estimation from sparse point clouds. Zero scalar curvature does not imply the full curvature tensor vanishes. Signs can reverse across source conventions, and coordinate-dependent estimator output is not automatically intrinsic curvature.



For the standard model spaces under the adopted convention:
\[
K_{\mathbb R^n}=0,
\qquad
K_{S_r^n}=\frac{1}{r^2},
\qquad
K_{H_r^n}=-\frac{1}{r^2}.
\]
In two dimensions \(S=2K\), but in higher dimensions scalar curvature aggregates many sectional curvatures. Consequently, one scalar can hide anisotropic positive and negative sectional behavior.
A cylinder in \(\mathbb R^3\) is visibly bent but has zero intrinsic Gaussian curvature, illustrating that extrinsic appearance does not determine intrinsic curvature.



Claims that latent neural geometry is curved require a declared metric, scale, estimator, uncertainty analysis, and comparison with flat or locally linear baselines.



At L2, Curvature connects the Riemann tensor, sectional planes, Ricci and scalar contractions, isometries, and model spaces while enforcing the distinction among intrinsic geometry, embeddings, dynamics, topology, and empirical estimation.

How biased are curvature estimates under noise and sparse sampling?
Does curvature improve prediction beyond linear and metric baselines?

Bianchi proofs, submanifold/Gauss equations, comparison theorems, topology-curvature theorems, and data estimators are intentionally deferred.

title: Circle / S¹
text:
The circle \(S^1\) is the topological space of points at unit distance from the origin in \(\mathbb R^2\), equivalently a periodic coordinate with endpoints identified.



\(S^1\) is the simplest compact space with a loop and is the basic model for phase, heading, and periodic latent variables. Its topology is not captured by treating angle as an ordinary interval with unrelated endpoints.



Moving continuously through angle \(2\pi\) returns to angle \(0\). There is no distinguished beginning or end.



Two equivalent descriptions are
\[
S^1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}
\]
with the subspace topology, and the quotient \(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\) identifying values that differ by an integer turn. The quotient coordinate \(t\pmod 1\) is measured in turns and maps to the embedded circle by
\[
[t]\longmapsto (\cos 2\pi t,\sin 2\pi t),
\qquad \theta=2\pi t
\]
when \(\theta\) is measured in radians. It is a one-dimensional smooth manifold and can be covered by local real-valued charts. Mrowka lists spheres as standard manifold examples (Mrowka 2004, sec. 1).




\(S^1\): circle.
\(\theta\pmod{2\pi}\): angular coordinate.
\(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\): quotient description.




Topology supplies quotient and continuity language. Manifold supplies its locally Euclidean interpretation.










Concept
Distinction




Interval
Has boundary endpoints; a circle identifies the periodic endpoints.


Limit cycle
A periodic orbit produced by dynamics; \(S^1\) is a space and need not be a trajectory or attractor.


Circular coordinate
A representation of values on \(S^1\); its observed distribution need not cover the full circle.


Ellipse
Topologically a circle but metrically and geometrically different under inherited coordinates.






A circular topology does not imply uniform speed, sinusoidal observations, a limit cycle, Euclidean circular geometry in data space, attraction, or a unique phase coordinate.



Time of day modulo 24 hours is circular: 23:59 is near 00:01 even though their scalar labels differ greatly.



Head direction, movement direction, and oscillatory phase may use circular variables. Evidence should distinguish circular state topology from periodic forcing or repeated observations.



\(S^1\) provides the first explicit non-Euclidean topology for testing latent representations and periodic dynamics.




How can circular topology be distinguished from a bent interval under noise?
Which phase coordinate is scientifically invariant?
How should incomplete traversal of \(S^1\) be analyzed?

Sutherland provides the inspected quotient and subspace-topology background (Sutherland 2024).

text: Moving continuously through angle \(2\pi\) returns to angle \(0\). There is no distinguished beginning or end.

title: Circle / S¹
text:
Two equivalent descriptions are
\[
S^1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}
\]
with the subspace topology, and the quotient \(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\) identifying values that differ by an integer turn. The quotient coordinate \(t\pmod 1\) is measured in turns and maps to the embedded circle by
\[
[t]\longmapsto (\cos 2\pi t,\sin 2\pi t),
\qquad \theta=2\pi t
\]
when \(\theta\) is measured in radians. It is a one-dimensional smooth manifold and can be covered by local real-valued charts. Mrowka lists spheres as standard manifold examples (Mrowka 2004, sec. 1).

title: Circle / S¹
text:
\(S^1\): circle.
\(\theta\pmod{2\pi}\): angular coordinate.
\(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\): quotient description.

title: Circle / S¹
text: Topology supplies quotient and continuity language. Manifold supplies its locally Euclidean interpretation.

title: Circle / S¹
text:
Concept
Distinction




Interval
Has boundary endpoints; a circle identifies the periodic endpoints.


Limit cycle
A periodic orbit produced by dynamics; \(S^1\) is a space and need not be a trajectory or attractor.


Circular coordinate
A representation of values on \(S^1\); its observed distribution need not cover the full circle.


Ellipse
Topologically a circle but metrically and geometrically different under inherited coordinates.

title: Circle / S¹
text: A circular topology does not imply uniform speed, sinusoidal observations, a limit cycle, Euclidean circular geometry in data space, attraction, or a unique phase coordinate.

title: Circle / S¹
text: Time of day modulo 24 hours is circular: 23:59 is near 00:01 even though their scalar labels differ greatly.

title: Circle / S¹
text: Head direction, movement direction, and oscillatory phase may use circular variables. Evidence should distinguish circular state topology from periodic forcing or repeated observations.

title: Circle / S¹
text: \(S^1\) provides the first explicit non-Euclidean topology for testing latent representations and periodic dynamics.

title: Ambient Dimension
text:
The ambient dimension is the dimension of the surrounding coordinate or vector space in which states, observations, or a candidate structure are represented.



Ambient dimension records how many coordinates the chosen representation provides, not how many degrees of freedom the represented system actually uses. Keeping those questions separate prevents high-dimensional recordings from being equated with high intrinsic complexity.



A curve drawn in three-dimensional space has ambient dimension three even though motion along the curve may require only one local coordinate.



If an object is represented as a subset \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^D\), then \(D\) is the ambient dimension of that representation. Changing the representation can change \(D\) without changing the underlying object.
For a data matrix with \(D\) measured features, \(D\) is often the observation-space ambient dimension. This does not make the observations a complete state.




\(\mathbb R^D\): ambient coordinate space.
\(D\): ambient dimension.
\(S\subseteq\mathbb R^D\): represented set.




State Space establishes that a space and its coordinates depend on a declared system description.










Concept
Distinction




Intrinsic dimension
Degrees of freedom assigned to the object under a model or criterion, not the surrounding coordinate count.


Number of observations
Sample count is not coordinate dimension.


Rank
A linear-algebraic property of a matrix or map that may be below ambient dimension.


State dimension
Dimension of a specified state representation; an observation space can have a different ambient dimension.






Ambient dimension does not imply intrinsic dimension, manifold structure, effective rank, independent coordinates, mechanistic variables, or adequate sampling of the space.



The unit circle represented in \(\mathbb R^2\) has ambient dimension two. The same circle embedded in \(\mathbb R^3\) has ambient dimension three although its local degree of freedom remains one.



The number of recorded neurons, sensors, time bins, or engineered features can define an ambient data dimension. It does not determine latent dimensionality.



Ambient Dimension supplies the reference quantity needed for careful claims about dimension reduction, subspaces, embeddings, and manifolds.




Which preprocessing steps change the declared ambient space?
Should missing or constrained coordinates count toward \(D\)?
Which representation is appropriate for cross-modal comparisons?





Levina and Bickel explicitly distinguish high-dimensional embedding from lower intrinsic dimension in their inspected estimator study (Levina and Bickel 2004).





Defines the surrounding coordinate-space dimension.
Separates ambient dimension from samples, rank, and intrinsic dimension.
States representation dependence.

title: Latent Dynamics & Geometry
text:
LDG is a version-controlled research-methodology knowledge system for latent states, dynamical systems, neural and behavioral dynamics, representation geometry, topology, dimensionality reduction, and multimodal modeling.
Its intended progression is:
This public site presents the scientific layer of the project: definitions, mathematical foundations, method descriptions, executable toy models, paper notes, and research questions. Internal planning and operational materials are intentionally not part of the published site.

title: Latent Dynamics & Geometry
text:
Start here

Concepts define the vocabulary for dynamics, latent variables, geometry, topology, and dimensionality.
Methods state each method’s problem, assumptions, learned and fixed quantities, failure modes, and baseline comparisons.
Math develops reusable formal objects and derivations.
Toy Models connect known generative structure to recovery and evaluation.
Papers and Research Questions organize evidence and open methodological problems.

title: Latent Dynamics & Geometry
text:
Reading policy
LDG distinguishes established definitions and results, source-author interpretations, project-level synthesis, and research hypotheses. Visualizations, low reconstruction error, decoding performance, temporal correlation, or a low-dimensional embedding are not treated as mechanistic evidence by themselves.

title: Attractor
text:
An attractor is an invariant dynamical set toward which states from a surrounding basin approach under the specified forward evolution, with any additional minimality or transitivity convention stated explicitly.



Attractors organize long-time behavior across many initial conditions. They may be fixed points, periodic orbits, or more complicated invariant sets. The term is also used inconsistently, so LDG must specify the adopted convention rather than label any frequently visited region an attractor.



An attractor is not merely a place where trajectories are often seen. It is a set that the dynamics preserves and toward which a nontrivial collection of nearby initial states evolves.



Let \((\mathcal X,d)\) be a metric state space and let \(I_x\) be the supported elapsed-time interval through \(x\). For a nonempty closed set \(\Lambda\subseteq\mathcal X\), define its forward basin (or forward stable set in Teschl’s terminology) by
\[
B^+(\Lambda)
=
\left\{
x\in\mathcal X:
[0,\infty)\subseteq I_x
\text{ and }
\lim_{t\to\infty}d(\phi_t(x),\Lambda)=0
\right\},
\]
where
\[
d(x,\Lambda)=\inf_{z\in\Lambda}d(x,z).
\]
The support condition prevents finite-time termination from being mistaken for long-time attraction. Convergence is to the set: it does not require convergence to one point, one phase, or a specified rate.
A set \(\Lambda\) is attracting when it is invariant and \(B^+(\Lambda)\) contains a neighborhood of \(\Lambda\). This is local attraction unless \(B^+(\Lambda)\) equals the declared full forward domain.


LDG follows Teschl’s convention for this object: under a complete two-sided flow, an attractor is a nonempty closed invariant attracting set that is also topologically transitive. Topological transitivity means that for any nonempty relatively open \(U,V\subseteq\Lambda\), there exists \(t\in\mathbb R\) such that
\[
\phi_t(U)\cap V\ne\varnothing.
\]
This added condition excludes attracting supersets that decompose into dynamically separate invariant pieces. It is one established convention, not the unique definition used throughout dynamics. Forward semiflows, stochastic systems, random attractors, and input-driven systems require separately declared variants (Teschl 2012, sec. 8.1).



A trapping region \(E\) is an open connected set with compact closure such that
\[
\phi_t(\overline E)\subset E,
\qquad t>0.
\]
Under Teschl’s complete-flow assumptions,
\[
\Lambda_E
=
\omega^+(E)
=
\bigcap_{t\ge0}\phi_t(\overline E)
\]
is a nonempty compact connected invariant attracting set (Teschl 2012, sec. 8.1). This is a sufficient construction of an attracting set, not a necessary characterization and not, by itself, proof of topological transitivity. The omega-limit and trapping-region proofs remain deferred.



Attraction and Lyapunov stability are different predicates. A point or set can be Lyapunov stable without attracting a neighborhood, and convergence toward a set does not by itself establish Lyapunov stability. When both properties are required, they must be checked separately using the Stability definitions.





\(\Lambda\): the candidate invariant set.
\(d(x,\Lambda)=\inf_{z\in\Lambda}d(x,z)\): distance from a point to the set.
\(I_x\): supported elapsed-time interval through \(x\).
\(B^+(\Lambda)\) or \(W^+(\Lambda)\): forward basin/stable set of \(\Lambda\).
\(E\): trapping region with compact closure.
\(\omega^+(E)\): forward omega-limit set of \(E\).
\(\phi_t\): forward evolution; a complete two-sided flow is required for the adopted transitivity convention.
\(t\to\infty\): the long-time limit in scope.




Stability supplies perturbation and closeness distinctions. Flow supplies finite-time evolution and supported domains across initial states. Metric supplies the distance-to-set construction.










Concept
Distinction




Attracting set
Has an invariant set with a neighborhood basin. Under the adopted convention it becomes an attractor only after topological transitivity is also established.


Lyapunov-stable object
Stability means nearby trajectories remain close; attraction concerns convergence toward a set. Either property can require separate verification.


Limit cycle
An attracting periodic orbit can be an attractor, but attractors need not be periodic.


Basin
The basin is the set of initial states approaching the attractor, not the attractor itself.


Frequently visited region
High occupancy can arise from sampling, noise, slow motion, or external input without invariance, a neighborhood basin, forward support, or transitivity.


Trapping-region limit set
A sufficient construction of a compact connected attracting set; it is not automatically transitive and therefore not automatically an attractor under the adopted convention.






An attractor does not imply:

that every initial state approaches it;
a unique attractor or basin;
a fixed point rather than a periodic or more complex set;
robustness to parameter changes or stochastic forcing;
that an empirical density peak is an attractor;
that finite trajectories identify the full basin;
that one trajectory approaching \(\Lambda\) establishes attraction from a neighborhood;
that recurrence, slow motion, clustering, decoding, low reconstruction error, or a density peak establishes invariance or transitivity;
that attraction implies Lyapunov stability or robustness to perturbations; or
that attraction explains the biological mechanism producing the data.




For \(\dot x=-x\), \(\Lambda=\{0\}\) is invariant and
\[
x(t)=x_0e^{-t}\longrightarrow0
\]
for every \(x_0\in\mathbb R\). Thus \(B^+(\Lambda)=\mathbb R\), and the singleton is topologically transitive, so it is a point attractor under the adopted convention.
By contrast, for \(\dot x=0\), every singleton is Lyapunov stable, but the basin of \(\{p\}\) is only \(\{p\}\) and does not contain a neighborhood in \(\mathbb R\); it is not an attractor. An attracting periodic orbit supplies a non-point example, but a repelling or merely isolated periodic orbit does not.



Attractor language is used for persistent activity, categorical decisions, memories, and recurring population states. A defensible claim requires evidence for an invariant model set and attraction from perturbed initial states, not only clustering, decoding, or repeated visitation.



At L2, Attractor provides an explicit basin, support condition, distance-to-set convergence, selected transitivity convention, and trapping-region construction. It preserves LDG’s prohibition against treating visualization, occupancy, recurrence, or one convergent trace as dynamical evidence.




Which attractor convention is appropriate for noisy or input-driven models?
How can basins be inferred from limited interventions and partial observations?
What baseline explanations should an attractor model beat?





Teschl develops forward stable sets/basins, attracting sets, trapping regions, and the adopted transitive attractor convention (Teschl 2012, sec. 8.1).
Teschl’s trapping-region and omega-limit proofs are cited as source context but are not reproduced in this Concept.

Separates attractor, basin, fixed point, limit cycle, and occupancy.
States empirical non-implications.
Types the basin with forward completeness and distance-to-set convergence.
Adopts and labels the attracting-plus-transitive convention.
Separates attracting sets, trapping-region limit sets, and transitive attractors.
Separates attraction from Lyapunov stability and empirical occupancy.

title: Convolution
text:
Convolution combines a signal with a shifted kernel by summing or integrating lag-weighted contributions to produce an output.



Convolution is the canonical input-output operation for linear time-invariant filters. It provides a fixed-kernel baseline against which latent state dynamics can be compared.



At each output time, align the kernel with the input history, multiply overlapping values, and add them. The kernel determines which lags matter and with what sign.



For scalar functions \(k,u:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\), continuous convolution is
\[
(k*u)(t)
=
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}k(\tau)u(t-\tau)\,d\tau,
\]
at times for which the integral exists. A common sufficient condition is \(k\in L^1(\mathbb R)\) with bounded \(u\); other \(L^p\) conditions are possible and must be declared. Compact support is useful only together with sufficient local integrability or boundedness; support alone does not guarantee the integral exists.
For sequences \(k=(k_m)\) and \(u=(u_m)\),
\[
(k*u)_n
=
\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}k_m u_{n-m},
\]
when the series converges. Absolute summability of one sequence together with boundedness of the other is one sufficient condition; finite-support sequences give a finite sum.


For scalar functions or sequences, when all required integrals/sums exist and rearrangement is justified,
\[
k*u=u*k,
\]
\[
(k_1*k_2)*u=k_1*(k_2*u),
\]
and convolution is distributive and linear in each argument. These identities require compatible domains and convergence conditions. Matrix multiplication is not commutative, so analogous matrix-valued operations must retain order.



For input \(u(t)\in\mathbb R^m\), output \(y(t)\in\mathbb R^q\), and kernel \(H(\tau)\in\mathbb R^{q\times m}\),
\[
y(t)
=
\int H(\tau)u(t-\tau)\,d\tau
\]
is dimensionally well typed. Each output channel is a sum of convolutions of input channels with the corresponding scalar kernel entries. The expression \(u*H\) is not generally an interchangeable commutative form because vector/matrix multiplication order and dimensions matter.



For a causal LTI system initialized at \(t_0\) with zero initial state and no direct feedthrough, the output has the zero-state response
\[
y_{\mathrm{zs}}(t)
=
\int_{t_0}^{t}H(t-s)u(s)\,ds
=
\int_{0}^{t-t_0}H(\tau)u(t-\tau)\,d\tau.
\]
Causality is represented by \(H(\tau)=0\) for \(\tau<0\). The full state-space output can additionally contain an initial-condition response and direct feedthrough:
\[
y(t)
=
Ce^{A(t-t_0)}x(t_0)
+
\int_{t_0}^{t}Ce^{A(t-s)}Bu(s)\,ds
+
Du(t).
\]
Thus \(H(\tau)=Ce^{A\tau}B\) for \(\tau>0\) gives the ordinary zero-state kernel. The term \(Du(t)\) must be kept separate or represented by a generalized impulse contribution \(D\delta(\tau)\); it is not an ordinary function-valued lag kernel (Åström and Murray 2021, sec. 6.3).









NoteEstablished Mathematical / Computational Background



Under one common convention, cross-correlation is
\[
(r_{ku})(t)=\int \overline{k(\tau)}u(\tau+t)\,d\tau,
\]
so it compares shifted alignment rather than applying the same reversal convention as convolution. Conventions vary, especially for complex signals, and must be stated.
Finite recorded arrays require boundary choices such as zero padding, periodic extension, reflection, truncation, or reporting only valid overlaps. Circular convolution produced by a discrete Fourier transform is not the same as linear convolution unless padding and indexing are chosen accordingly. FFT multiplication is an implementation of convolution under stated transform/boundary conventions, not the definition of convolution.







\(k\): scalar kernel or impulse response.
\(H(\tau)\in\mathbb R^{q\times m}\): matrix-valued kernel.
\(u(t)\in\mathbb R^m\): input signal.
\(y(t)\in\mathbb R^q\): convolved output.
\(y_{\mathrm{zs}}\): zero-state response.
\(\tau\) or \(m\): lag variable.




Kernel defines the lag-dependent weighting function.










Concept
Distinction




Correlation
Compares shifted alignment under a declared conjugation/reversal convention; it is not automatically the same operation as convolution.


Circular convolution
Uses periodic indexing, as in an unpadded DFT implementation. Linear convolution requires appropriate padding or another boundary convention.


FFT multiplication
A computational method under transform and boundary assumptions, not the mathematical definition.


Filtering
A broader operation; LTI filtering is represented by convolution.


Kernel
The weighting function; convolution is the operation using it.


State-space response
May include initial-state response and direct feedthrough in addition to the zero-state convolution term.


Smoothing
One possible effect of particular kernels. Convolution kernels can also differentiate, delay, oscillate, or amplify.






Convolution does not imply causality, finite memory, invertibility, a known kernel, smoothing, stable dynamics, a particular boundary convention, linear biological mechanism, or that all time dependence is captured by a fixed filter. Algebraic identities do not apply when the relevant sums/integrals diverge or dimensions are incompatible.



With discrete kernel \(k=(1/2,1/2)\),
\[
y_n=\tfrac12u_n+\tfrac12u_{n-1},
\]
so the output averages the current and previous inputs. This smoothing loses some rapidly varying information.



Convolution appears in temporal receptive fields, sensor responses, smoothing, and hemodynamic models. Predictive success of a convolutional model does not establish hidden recurrent dynamics.



At L2, Convolution gives LDG explicit existence, dimensional, algebraic, causal, initial-condition, and direct-feedthrough boundaries for the fixed-kernel alternative before deconvolution or more complex latent temporal models.




When is time invariance defensible?
How should boundary conditions and irregular sampling be handled?
Which kernels are distinguishable from available inputs?





Åström and Murray provide the inspected LTI initial-condition, zero-state convolution, impulse-response, and direct-feedthrough formulations (Åström and Murray 2021, sec. 6.3). Section numbering was checked against the inspected 24 July 2020 electronic second-edition manuscript corresponding to the published edition.
Transform theorems, distribution theory, FFT algorithms, and numerical boundary-analysis proofs are intentionally deferred.

For sequences \(k=(k_m)\) and \(u=(u_m)\),
\[
(k*u)_n
=
\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}k_m u_{n-m},
\]
when the series converges. Absolute summability of one sequence together with boundedness of the other is one sufficient condition; finite-support sequences give a finite sum.


For scalar functions or sequences, when all required integrals/sums exist and rearrangement is justified,
\[
k*u=u*k,
\]
\[
(k_1*k_2)*u=k_1*(k_2*u),
\]
and convolution is distributive and linear in each argument. These identities require compatible domains and convergence conditions. Matrix multiplication is not commutative, so analogous matrix-valued operations must retain order.



For input \(u(t)\in\mathbb R^m\), output \(y(t)\in\mathbb R^q\), and kernel \(H(\tau)\in\mathbb R^{q\times m}\),
\[
y(t)
=
\int H(\tau)u(t-\tau)\,d\tau
\]
is dimensionally well typed. Each output channel is a sum of convolutions of input channels with the corresponding scalar kernel entries. The expression \(u*H\) is not generally an interchangeable commutative form because vector/matrix multiplication order and dimensions matter.



For a causal LTI system initialized at \(t_0\) with zero initial state and no direct feedthrough, the output has the zero-state response
\[
y_{\mathrm{zs}}(t)
=
\int_{t_0}^{t}H(t-s)u(s)\,ds
=
\int_{0}^{t-t_0}H(\tau)u(t-\tau)\,d\tau.
\]
Causality is represented by \(H(\tau)=0\) for \(\tau<0\). The full state-space output can additionally contain an initial-condition response and direct feedthrough:
\[
y(t)
=
Ce^{A(t-t_0)}x(t_0)
+
\int_{t_0}^{t}Ce^{A(t-s)}Bu(s)\,ds
+
Du(t).
\]
Thus \(H(\tau)=Ce^{A\tau}B\) for \(\tau>0\) gives the ordinary zero-state kernel. The term \(Du(t)\) must be kept separate or represented by a generalized impulse contribution \(D\delta(\tau)\); it is not an ordinary function-valued lag kernel (Åström and Murray 2021, sec. 6.3).









NoteEstablished Mathematical / Computational Background



Under one common convention, cross-correlation is
\[
(r_{ku})(t)=\int \overline{k(\tau)}u(\tau+t)\,d\tau,
\]
so it compares shifted alignment rather than applying the same reversal convention as convolution. Conventions vary, especially for complex signals, and must be stated.
Finite recorded arrays require boundary choices such as zero padding, periodic extension, reflection, truncation, or reporting only valid overlaps. Circular convolution produced by a discrete Fourier transform is not the same as linear convolution unless padding and indexing are chosen accordingly. FFT multiplication is an implementation of convolution under stated transform/boundary conventions, not the definition of convolution.

title: Deconvolution
text:
Deconvolution is the inverse problem of estimating an unknown input, source, or kernel from observations modeled as a convolution, usually in the presence of noise and incomplete information.



Convolution can smooth or suppress components of a signal. Recovering what preceded that filtering is often unstable: small observation errors can produce large changes in a naive inverse.



If a sensor blurs a sharp event with a known response kernel, deconvolution tries to infer the event that could have produced the blurred measurement. Multiple sources may fit nearly equally well once noise is present.



Let \(\mathcal U\) be a source space, \(\mathcal K\) a kernel space, and \(\mathcal Y\) an observation space. For a fixed kernel \(k\), define the convolution operator
\[
K_k:\mathcal U\to\mathcal Y,
\qquad
K_k u=k*u.
\]
The observed data follow a forward model such as
\[
y=K_k u+v,
\]
where \(v\) is observation noise under a declared observation law. Known-kernel deconvolution estimates \(u\) with \(k\) fixed. Blind deconvolution estimates both \(u\) and \(k\) and therefore has additional scaling, shift, boundary, and factorization ambiguities. Blind recovery is not identifiable without constraints that restrict these equivalences.


If \(K_k u_1=K_k u_2\), then the data cannot distinguish \(u_1\) and \(u_2\). Equivalently, their difference lies in the null space,
\[
u_1-u_2\in\ker K_k.
\]
Even when the null space is trivial, small singular values or nearly suppressed frequency components can make the inverse ill-conditioned: small perturbations in \(y\) produce large changes in a naive recovered source. Injectivity, stable inversion, and numerical conditioning are separate properties.



Under transform and boundary conditions for which convolution becomes multiplication,
\[
\widehat y(\omega)
=
\widehat k(\omega)\widehat u(\omega)
+
\widehat v(\omega).
\]
The formal inverse
\[
\widehat u(\omega)
=
\frac{\widehat y(\omega)}{\widehat k(\omega)}
\]
is defined only where \(\widehat k(\omega)\ne0\). If \(|\widehat k(\omega)|\) is small, the noise term is amplified by \(1/|\widehat k(\omega)|\). Zeros erase those components under the stated model. Finite windows, sampling, aliasing, padding, and circular-versus-linear convolution further change the implemented operator, so transform division is not a universal exact inverse.



A common regularized estimator is
\[
\widehat u_\lambda
\in
\arg\min_{u\in\mathcal U}
\left\{
\mathcal D(K_k u,y)
+
\lambda\mathcal R(u)
\right\},
\]
where \(\mathcal D\) is a data-fit or negative-log-likelihood term and \(\mathcal R\) encodes assumptions such as smoothness, sparsity, nonnegativity, or bounded variation. Regularization can stabilize inversion but introduces bias toward the preferred solution class. Different penalties or priors can select different sources that fit the data similarly.
A probabilistic formulation combines an observation likelihood and prior,
\[
p(u\mid y,k)
\propto
p(y\mid K_k u)\,p(u).
\]
A posterior or MAP estimate is conditional on those choices; it is not assumption-free recovery.
For blind deconvolution one may optimize over \((u,k)\),
\[
\min_{u,k}
\mathcal D(K_k u,y)
+
\lambda_u\mathcal R_u(u)
+
\lambda_k\mathcal R_k(k),
\]
but scale and shift conventions, kernel normalization/support, positivity, and other identifiability constraints must be declared.



A small forward residual \(\|K_k\widehat u-y\|\) checks consistency with the observation but does not prove source recovery. In a toy model with known ground truth, evaluation should separately report source error, event/support recovery, timing error, kernel error when estimated, and sensitivity to noise, sampling, boundaries, and regularization. Without ground truth, held-out forward prediction, calibration, interventions, or multiple observation channels provide indirect evidence only and cannot establish a unique source.
Richardson’s inspected paper supplies a primary convolutional image-restoration example, demonstrates sensitivity to noise and boundaries, and describes an iterative approximation without a general convergence proof (Richardson 1972). The general inverse-operator and regularization framing above is established inverse-problem background, not attributed solely to that algorithm.





\(\mathcal U,\mathcal K,\mathcal Y\): source, kernel, and observation spaces.
\(K_k:\mathcal U\to\mathcal Y\): convolution forward operator for kernel \(k\).
\(y\): observed convolved signal.
\(u\): unknown source or input.
\(k\): known or estimated kernel.
\(v\): observation noise.
\(\widehat u\): recovered source estimate.
\(\ker K_k\): source perturbations invisible to the forward operator.
\(\mathcal D\): data-fit or negative-log-likelihood term.
\(\mathcal R\): regularizer or prior penalty.
\(\lambda\): regularization strength.




Convolution supplies the forward operator. Observation Noise supplies the measurement uncertainty that makes inversion fragile.










Concept
Distinction




Inverse filtering
A direct inverse construction; deconvolution is the broader inverse problem and may require regularization or probabilistic inference.


Blind deconvolution
Both source and kernel are unknown, adding scale, shift, boundary, and factorization ambiguities that require explicit constraints.


Denoising
Removes or models noise without necessarily undoing a convolution operator.


Source separation
Separates multiple contributing sources; it is not automatically a convolution inverse.


Causal/mechanistic recovery
Claims a physical generator or cause. Mathematical recovery under a forward model does not establish this interpretation.


System identification
Estimates a system or kernel; deconvolution may instead assume the kernel and estimate the input.






Deconvolution does not imply exact recovery, a unique or stable inverse, a correct known kernel, identifiable blind factors, separation of signal from structured noise, unbiased regularization, or recovery of a biological cause from a measurement trace. A low forward residual can coexist with large source error.



Let the discrete kernel be \(k=(1/2,1/2)\), so
\[
y_n=\frac{u_n+u_{n-1}}{2}+v_n.
\]
For the alternating component \(u_n=(-1)^n\), the noiseless convolution is zero because adjacent values cancel. That component lies in the null space under an infinite/periodic idealization and cannot be recovered from \(y\). Components near that alternating frequency are strongly attenuated, so division amplifies noise.
A smoothness-regularized estimate can suppress the amplified component and improve stability, but it may also erase a true sharp event. Source error and forward fit must therefore be evaluated separately.



Examples include estimating neural events from calcium fluorescence or latent neural activity from a hemodynamic response. Recovery quality depends on kernel validity, sampling, noise, and prior assumptions.



At L2, Deconvolution provides a typed inverse-operator baseline with explicit identifiability, conditioning, regularization, and evaluation limits before recovered time courses are interpreted as latent states, dynamics, or mechanisms.

title: Embedding
text:
An embedding is an injective map that represents one space inside another while preserving the declared structure strongly enough that the original object can be recovered from its image.



Embedding language distinguishes a faithful representation of an object from a projection or visualization that may collapse distinct points or distort relevant structure.



A circle can be placed in the plane without self-identifying points. Mapping the same circle onto a line with overlaps would not faithfully embed it.



At the topological level, a map \(e:X\to Y\) is an embedding when it is injective and gives a homeomorphism between \(X\) and its image \(e(X)\) with the subspace topology. Smooth embeddings add smoothness and an injective derivative.
This L1 object uses only the representation principle; full topology and differential conditions belong to later objects. Whitney’s classical work establishes broad smooth embedding results for differentiable manifolds (Whitney 1936).




\(X\): source space.
\(Y\): ambient target space.
\(e:X\hookrightarrow Y\): embedding.
\(e(X)\): embedded image.




State Space supplies the source object whose states may be represented. Ambient Dimension supplies the target-space coordinate count.
Assumed background: functions, injectivity, and elementary continuity.










Concept
Distinction




Projection
May collapse distinct points and need not preserve the source structure.


Dimensionality reduction
An algorithmic goal; its output is not automatically a mathematical embedding.


Feature map
Any map to features; injectivity or structural preservation may be absent.


Manifold
A type of space that may be embedded; an embedding does not prove the data form a manifold.






An embedding does not imply isometry, low distortion under a chosen metric, unique coordinates, causal or mechanistic meaning, a manifold source, or successful recovery from finite noisy samples.



The map
\[
e(\theta)=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)
\]
represents the abstract circle in \(\mathbb R^2\) when \(\theta\) is understood modulo \(2\pi\). The coordinate image has ambient dimension two but one intrinsic circular degree of freedom.



Learned low-dimensional coordinates are often called embeddings. LDG requires specifying whether “embedding” is only an algorithmic label or a supported claim of injective structural preservation.



Embedding prepares precise manifold and topology language while preventing nonlinear visualization from being treated as evidence by itself.

What distortions matter for dynamics and behavior?
